title: Bridging Finance for Care Home Acquisitions
excerpt: Bridging loans help buyers complete care home purchases fast, bridging the gap between exchange and a regulated commercial mortgage while CQC registration is sorted out.
metaTitle: Bridging Finance for Care Home Acquisitions
metaDescription: How bridging loans fund care home purchases before CQC registration completes, what lenders want to see, and how to exit onto a commercial mortgage.
keywords: bridging loans for care homes, care home acquisition finance, CQC registration funding, short-term property finance care sector, developer finance care home conversion, care home bridging loan lenders, exit to commercial mortgage care home
author: Mark Higgins
content:
Bridging loans for care home acquisition give buyers the speed to exchange and complete on a regulated care home before CQC registration, staffing transfer or a full commercial mortgage is in place. Businesses use bridging loans for care home acquisition when a purchase needs to move faster than a standard healthcare lender can underwrite, typically completing in two to four weeks against a clear exit onto a term mortgage. To understand the fundamentals first, our guide to what bridging finance actually involves is a useful starting point.

What this means in practice

In practice, care home purchases rarely fit neatly into a normal commercial mortgage timeline. A term lender wants trading accounts, CQC registration confirmed in the new owner's name, and often a track record of running a similar facility. None of that exists on day one of a purchase, which is exactly the gap short-term property finance fills.

We see two distinct buyer types. The first is an operator already registered with the CQC buying a second or third home, where the bridging loan simply speeds up completion while the mortgage lender finishes its checks. The second is a first-time care home buyer, sometimes a healthcare professional or an investor backing an experienced manager, who needs to complete before their CQC application is even submitted.

The distinction between a trading and non-trading care home matters enormously. A trading home with residents in situ, current fee income and an existing registration differs fundamentally from an empty building bought with the intention of converting or reopening it. Lenders price and structure these very differently, and getting this wrong at application stage is one of the quickest ways to see a deal stall.

There's also a third group worth mentioning: the buyer already mid-portfolio who spots an opportunity through an off-market introduction from an agent. These deals often come with tight vendor deadlines because the seller wants certainty and speed rather than the highest headline price. A bridging loan lets a buyer compete on those terms without waiting for a mortgage offer that might take two months to land. Buyers based in the capital exploring this route can find more detail in our overview of bridging loans in London.

Vendors in the care sector are frequently retiring operators or families dealing with probate, and they tend to favour whoever can actually complete rather than whoever offers the most. This is where a bridging facility can genuinely win a deal that would otherwise go to a cash buyer or a larger corporate operator with pre-arranged funding lines. If you're weighing up costs at this stage, comparing current bridging loan rates across the UK before approaching a lender makes good sense.

If you're ready to explore options for your own purchase, you can get a bridging loan quote and get a sense of what's achievable within your timeline.

How it works

The mechanics are similar to any bridging loan, but the security and exit strategy carry more weight than usual. The lender takes a first charge over the care home property and assesses the purchase price against a valuation that reflects both bricks and mortar and, where relevant, the trading value of the business itself.

Loan-to-value tends to sit lower for care homes than standard residential or commercial bridging loans, commonly in the 55% to 65% range against open market value, sometimes lower still for non-trading or partially vacant homes. Interest is usually retained or added to the loan rather than serviced monthly, which matters because a home mid-transition often has limited or no income during the bridge period.

The exit is the part underwriters scrutinise hardest. That might be a refinance onto a specialist healthcare mortgage once CQC registration and a trading history of three to six months are in place, a sale of the business as a going concern, or in some cases a cash exit from a wider portfolio refinance. Lenders require this mapped out in writing before they commit, rather than left as a vague intention.

Arrangement fees on care home bridging tend to run from 1.5% to 2% of the loan, with exit fees either waived or set at around 1%, depending on the lender and whether interest is retained or serviced. Valuation fees for care homes are higher than for standard commercial property because they require a specialist healthcare surveyor, and it's not unusual to see this cost £2,500 to £6,000 depending on bed numbers and location.

Legal costs also tend to run higher than a typical commercial bridge because solicitors must review the CQC position, any staff TUPE implications, and existing local authority or NHS placement contracts. We always tell clients to budget for legal fees in the region of £8,000 to £15,000 all in, covering both their own solicitor and the lender's legal costs, which the borrower usually pays either way.

Term length is typically 6 to 12 months, occasionally stretching to 18 months where a refurbishment or CQC registration change is involved. Most lenders build in an option to extend by a few months if the exit is delayed slightly, though this usually comes with an extension fee and a fresh review of the exit plan.

Typical scenarios

A care home operator in the Midlands identified a 34-bed home coming to market at £1.85 million. Her existing healthcare mortgage lender needed eight weeks to underwrite a new facility, but the vendor's other buyer had already fallen through once and wanted completion in three weeks. We arranged a bridging loan of £1,110,000 against the £1.85 million valuation, a 60% LTV, over a 9-month term with interest retained. Funds released in 16 working days, and she refinanced onto a five-year healthcare mortgage once her CQC variation was approved and three months of trading accounts were available. Operators in the Midlands considering a similar route can also look at bridging loans in Birmingham for local context.

A separate scenario involved a first-time buyer purchasing a non-trading 22-bed home for £780,000, intending to refurbish two wings and reopen under new registration. This sat closer to developer finance than a standard acquisition bridge. We placed £468,000, a 60% LTV, over 12 months, with a drawdown facility for refurbishment costs released in stages. The exit was a sale to an established operator once planning consent for the extension was secured, and the deal completed in 19 working days from instruction. A similar buyer looking at bridging loans in Norwich would follow much the same structure.

A third example worth including is a portfolio operator buying a struggling 40-bed home out of administration for £2.1 million, where the previous owner's CQC rating sat at Requires Improvement. Standard mortgage lenders wouldn't touch it until the rating improved, so we arranged a bridge of £1,155,000 at 55% LTV over 12 months. The buyer's existing management team took over operations immediately, and within five months the CQC rating had moved to Good, at which point a healthcare lender refinanced the position comfortably. Buyers exploring opportunities via bridging loans in Reading often face comparable timelines.

Each of these cases shows the same pattern: a genuine timing gap between what the seller needs and what a mainstream lender can deliver quickly enough. Short-term property finance doesn't replace the long-term funding; it simply buys the time needed to get the paperwork, registration or trading history into a shape that a mortgage lender will accept.

What lenders look for

Lenders assess care home bridging applications on security, sector experience and the credibility of the exit, in that order. A weak exit strategy is the single biggest reason applications stall or get declined outright.

Expect LTVs of 55% to 65% on trading homes with clean CQC ratings, dropping to 45% to 55% on non-trading stock or homes with an inadequate CQC rating that needs turning around. Timescales from enquiry to funds typically run 10 to 20 working days where legal title and valuation are straightforward, though anything involving a change of CQC registration mid-transaction can push this out.

Security is almost always a first charge over the freehold, with lenders wanting an up-to-date valuation from a surveyor experienced in healthcare property, not a generic commercial valuer. Evidence of the exit must be concrete: a signed mortgage offer in principle, a business sale agreement, or a refinance illustration from a named healthcare lender, not simply a statement of intent.

Sector experience matters more here than in most bridging applications. A first-time buyer isn't automatically declined, but lenders will want to see a strong registered manager in place, a clear operational plan, and often some evidence of care sector background somewhere in the buying structure, whether that's the buyer themselves or a partner they've brought in.

Personal guarantees are standard on care home bridging loans, and lenders will also look closely at the buyer's exit contacts. Do they already have a relationship with a healthcare mortgage broker or lender lined up, or are they starting that conversation from scratch. The former moves much faster through underwriting than the latter.

Staffing continuity is another point lenders quietly weigh up, even though it doesn't appear on the application form directly. A home where the existing care staff and registered manager are staying on presents a much lower operational risk than one where the entire team is leaving at completion, and this can influence both pricing and the lender's appetite to proceed at all.

From a broker's point of view, the deals that complete fastest are the ones where the buyer has already had an honest conversation with a healthcare mortgage lender about their refinance before the bridging application even goes in. Walking into a bridging conversation with that reassurance already in place changes the whole tone of underwriting, because the lender isn't being asked to take a leap of faith on the exit; they're being shown one that's already partly agreed.

Our advice to anyone considering this route is to start the exit conversation early, get a specialist healthcare valuer involved from the outset, and be realistic about the CQC timeline for your specific registration change. Care home bridging can move remarkably fast when the fundamentals are right, but it punishes vague planning more than most areas of commercial finance. It's also worth reviewing our roundup of leading bridging loan lenders in the UK when shortlisting who to approach.

Key risks to consider

As with any short-term property finance, the biggest risk is exit failure, meaning the planned refinance, sale or portfolio refinance doesn't materialise on schedule. This is why lenders scrutinise the exit so closely at application stage, and why borrowers should have a fallback plan, not just a primary one, before committing to a bridging loan.

CQC timelines can also slip beyond expectations, particularly where a registration change or new manager application is involved. Building in a buffer against the loan term, rather than assuming the shortest possible CQC turnaround, helps avoid the need for a costly extension. Staffing disruption, unexpected repair costs on an older building, or a slower-than-expected recovery in occupancy can all affect the trading position a refinance lender will want to see, so it pays to stress-test the numbers conservatively before committing.

Frequently Asked Questions

How quickly can a bridging loan for a care home acquisition complete?
Most care home bridging loans complete in two to four weeks from application, though straightforward cases with clean legal title and a specialist valuation already in hand can move faster, sometimes in as little as 16 working days.

What loan-to-value can I expect on a care home bridging loan?
Trading care homes with a clean CQC rating typically achieve 55% to 65% LTV against open market value, while non-trading or partially vacant homes, or those with a weaker CQC rating, tend to see 45% to 55%.

Can I get a bridging loan for a care home without CQC registration in place?
Yes, this is one of the most common uses of bridging finance in the sector, since it allows a buyer to complete the purchase before their CQC application is approved, with a refinance onto a healthcare mortgage planned once registration and trading history are in place.

What exit strategies do lenders accept for care home bridging loans?
Common exits include refinancing onto a specialist healthcare mortgage once CQC registration and a trading history of three to six months are established, selling the business as a going concern, or a cash exit from a wider portfolio refinance.

How much do care home bridging loans cost in fees?
Arrangement fees typically run from 1.5% to 2% of the loan, with exit fees either waived or around 1%. Specialist healthcare valuations usually cost £2,500 to £6,000, and legal fees tend to fall between £8,000 and £15,000 in total.

Can a first-time care home buyer get a bridging loan?
Yes, though lenders will want to see a strong registered manager in place, a clear operational plan, and some evidence of care sector experience within the buying structure, even if the buyer themselves is new to the sector.

How long is the typical term for a care home bridging loan?
Terms usually run 6 to 12 months, occasionally extending to 18 months where refurbishment or a CQC registration change is involved, with most lenders allowing a short extension if the exit is slightly delayed.

If you'd like tailored guidance on structuring your purchase, you can speak to a bridging specialist or explore our full range of funding solutions to see how bridging fits alongside other options.

title: Bridging Loans for Company Directors
excerpt: Company directors face different affordability checks when applying for bridging loans. Here is how lenders assess director applicants, what evidence you need, and how to get approved fast.
metaTitle: Bridging Loans for Company Directors
metaDescription: Bridging Loans for Company Directors. Expert advice from Boxx Commercial Finance, a whole-of-market UK bridging finance broker.
keywords: bridging loans for company directors, director bridging loan uk, short-term property finance for directors, bridging loan self employed director, company director property finance, developer finance for directors, bridging loans UK company owners
author: Andrew Farrimond
content:
A bridging loan company director UK applicant is assessed differently from a PAYE employee, because lenders look at company accounts, dividend history and director's loan accounts rather than a payslip. Bridging loans for company directors are used to buy property quickly, break a chain, fund a refurbishment, or release equity while a business's main income sits inside the company rather than the individual's personal bank account. Directors often qualify faster than expected once a lender understands the structure.

We arrange this type of borrowing every week at Boxx Commercial Finance, and the pattern is always the same. Directors assume their income looks complicated to a lender. In reality, bridging lenders care far less about how your income is structured than a mainstream mortgage lender does, because the loan is secured against property and the exit route matters more than your payslip history. If you want a clearer grounding in how this type of lending works before going further, our guide on what bridging finance actually involves is a useful starting point.

What surprises most directors is how much faster the conversation moves once a specialist lender is involved rather than a high street bank. High street underwriters are trained to fit applicants into standard boxes, and a director who pays himself a low salary and takes dividends irregularly simply does not fit. Bridging lenders, by contrast, spend their entire working week looking at exactly this profile, so the questions they ask are sharper and more relevant, and the decisions come back quicker.

What this means in practice

In practice, being a company director changes the paperwork a lender wants, not whether you can get a bridging loan at all. Most bridging lenders will look at your last two years of company accounts, your SA302s or tax year overviews, and sometimes a reference from your accountant confirming the business is trading normally.

If you take a modest salary and leave profit in the business, some lenders will still want to understand the full picture, because they need comfort that you can service any interest that is not added to the loan, and that your exit strategy stacks up. Directors of limited companies who take irregular dividends sometimes get a harder time from high street banks, but specialist bridging lenders are built for exactly this scenario.

This is also where structure matters. If you are borrowing personally to buy a residential property, the lender assesses you as an individual with director income. If the loan is for a commercial or investment purchase through your limited company, the lender may want personal guarantees from directors regardless of the company's own trading position. Either way, the loan is secured on the property first and foremost, and your director status is really a question of how you evidence income and repayment ability.

Lenders draw a distinction between a director who owns 100% of a trading company and a director who holds a minority shareholding in a larger business. A sole director with full control tends to get a simpler underwriting process, because there is only one set of accounts and one person's intentions to assess. A minority director, say someone holding 20% of a firm with three other shareholders, may find the lender wants sight of the shareholder agreement, or wants to understand whether other directors need to consent to any borrowing that touches company assets.

Another point that catches directors out is how a lender treats retained profit sitting on the balance sheet. Many directors assume that £150,000 or £200,000 of retained earnings automatically strengthens their application, and to a point it does, because it shows the business is healthy. But lenders will want to know whether that cash is actually accessible, or whether it is tied up in stock, work in progress, or committed to supplier payments. A conversation with your accountant before you apply, about how much of that cash could genuinely be extracted as a dividend if needed, saves a lot of back and forth later. If you're weighing up options at this stage, you can get a bridging loan quote before committing to a particular lender.

How it works

A bridging loan works by using the property itself, plus your exit plan, as the main security for short-term lending, typically over 1 to 18 months. For a director, the process starts the same way as any applicant: valuation of the security property, a credit check, and an assessment of the exit route, whether that is sale, refinance onto a term mortgage, or repayment from company funds.

Where it differs is the underwriting on affordability. Lenders will ask to see your latest set of filed accounts at Companies House, plus more recent management accounts if the filed set is more than a few months old. They will often ask your accountant to confirm, in writing, that the business is solvent and trading as expected. Some lenders will also want to see the director's loan account, particularly if you plan to draw funds from the company to service interest or repay the loan.

Rates for director-led bridging loans currently sit broadly in line with the wider bridging market, and current UK bridging loan rates are worth checking before you commit, since pricing varies more between lenders than most people expect. Fees typically include an arrangement fee of around 1-2%, a valuation fee, and legal costs on both sides. Interest is usually charged monthly and can be serviced, retained, or rolled up into the loan, which matters a great deal if your income is dividend-based and irregular.

For most director applicants we deal with, monthly interest rates on first charge bridging loans sit somewhere between 0.55% and 0.85%, with second charge loans, or those against commercial and semi-commercial property, running slightly higher, often between 0.75% and 1.1% a month. On a £300,000 loan, that difference between the low end and high end of pricing can easily mean an extra £900 to £1,200 a month in interest, so it is worth having a broker shop the whole market rather than accepting the first offer from a single lender. Reviewing a list of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK can also help you understand where director-friendly criteria tend to sit.

Legal costs are another area directors underestimate. Because the lender's solicitor and your own solicitor both need to review company accounts, articles of association, and sometimes a shareholder agreement, legal fees on a director-led bridging loan can run £500 to £1,000 higher than a straightforward personal application. Building this into your costings early avoids an unpleasant surprise at completion.

Typical scenarios

Two scenarios come up repeatedly with director clients, one residential and one development-led.

A company director in Reading found a house he wanted to buy but his own sale had fallen through three weeks before exchange. He needed £310,000 against a property valued at £520,000, a loan-to-value of 60%, over a 7 month term, exiting on the sale of his existing home once a new buyer was found. Because his accounts showed consistent dividends over two years, the lender was comfortable with rolled-up interest. Funds completed in 11 working days, and this is a common pattern we see for bridging loans in Reading where chain breaks are the main driver.

A second client, a property developer and sole director of his own construction firm, needed £420,000 to complete a part-finished conversion of a former commercial unit into four flats near Birmingham. The property was valued at £700,000 in its current state, giving 60% LTV, over a 12 month term. His exit was refinance onto a buy-to-let term facility once the units were let. Because this involved development finance, the lender wanted a schedule of works, a QS report at drawdown stages, and evidence of build cost contingency. The deal completed in 19 working days, slower than a straightforward residential case because of the staged drawdowns, which is typical for developer finance secured through bridging loans for company directors in this position, a pattern that also holds for bridging loans in Birmingham more generally.

A third scenario worth mentioning involves a director who wanted to buy the freehold of the commercial unit her business already traded from, rather than continuing to rent. She needed £185,000 against a valuation of £280,000, giving 66% LTV, over a 9 month bridging term while a commercial mortgage application was processed in the background. Because the loan was effectively self-funding, with the company paying rent to itself instead of a landlord, the lender treated the affordability assessment as straightforward, and the case completed in 14 working days once the accountant confirmed the company's rent history and profit trend, a scenario similar to cases we've handled for bridging loans in London and bridging loans in Norwich.

What lenders look for

Lenders want clear evidence of the exit, sufficient security value, and enough visibility into a director's financial position to be confident interest will be serviced or the loan repaid on time. Loan-to-value for director-led bridging loans typically ranges from 65% to 75% on residential security and 60% to 65% on commercial or semi-commercial property, though some specialist lenders will stretch to 80% with additional security or a stronger exit.

Timescales from enquiry to funds usually run between 10 and 21 working days for straightforward cases, and can extend to 4-6 weeks where development drawdowns, planning conditions, or complex company structures are involved. Acceptable security includes residential property, buy-to-let, semi-commercial and, less commonly, land with planning consent.

Evidence of exit is where most director applications either sail through or stall. Lenders want a mortgage in principle for refinance exits, an estate agent's valuation and marketing evidence for sale exits, or a clear repayment source from company funds with an accountant's confirmation. The most common reason we see director applications declined is an unclear or unrealistic exit, closely followed by directors underestimating how long a company sale or refinance will actually take once due diligence is factored in. A third recurring issue is directors of newly incorporated companies, under 18 months trading, being asked for personal guarantees or additional security because the business has no track record yet.

Credit history matters too, both personal and business. A director with a clean personal credit file but a company that has had a County Court Judgment, even a small one that was paid promptly, will usually need to explain the circumstances. Lenders are generally understanding about one-off issues, particularly late payments caused by a client paying the business late, but a pattern of missed payments or an unsatisfied CCJ will make most mainstream bridging lenders nervous, pushing the case towards a smaller pool of specialist lenders who price for that extra risk.

Lenders also look closely at how many other companies a director is involved with. Serial entrepreneurs who sit as director across five or six different limited companies sometimes find the underwriting takes longer, simply because the lender wants to check none of those other companies has outstanding County Court Judgments, winding-up petitions, or unfiled accounts that might reflect on the director's overall reliability. Being upfront about this from the start, rather than letting the lender discover it during a Companies House search, speeds things up considerably.

Common mistakes

The single biggest mistake is applying before speaking to an accountant about how the accounts will be presented to a lender. Directors often assume the lender will simply take the figures at face value, when in reality a short covering letter from the accountant, explaining a one-off dip in profit or a large dividend taken for a specific purpose, can be the difference between an instant yes and weeks of back and forth queries.

A second common mistake is underestimating how long a company-funded exit actually takes. Directors sometimes plan to repay a bridging loan from a dividend, without factoring in that the company needs sufficient distributable reserves, that the dividend itself needs formal paperwork, and that moving large sums out of a business can trigger its own tax and timing questions. Building in a realistic buffer of four to six weeks beyond the expected repayment date avoids the loan running into default territory unnecessarily.

A third mistake, and one we see surprisingly often, is directors applying to several bridging lenders directly at the same time in the hope of speeding things up. Each application usually triggers its own credit search and its own set of document requests, which slows everything down and can make a director's file look less coherent, not more. Working with one broker who understands the director's structure and approaches the right two or three lenders tends to produce a faster, cleaner outcome than a scattergun approach.

Finally, some directors leave the exit route too vague, describing it simply as sale of property or refinance without any supporting evidence. Lenders want to see that groundwork has already started, whether that is a mortgage broker actively working on a refinance, or an estate agent already marketing a property. A vague exit plan, even a sensible one, is far more likely to trigger extra conditions or a lower loan-to-value than one backed by paperwork from day one.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a company director get a bridging loan if their salary is low?
Yes. Lenders look at overall company performance, dividend history and retained profit, not just PAYE salary, so a low salary with irregular dividends is not usually a barrier.

Do I need two years of company accounts to qualify?
Most lenders prefer two years of filed accounts, but newer companies can still qualify, often with additional security or a personal guarantee to offset the lack of trading history.

Will a County Court Judgment against my company stop me getting a bridging loan?
Not automatically. A small, promptly paid CCJ is usually explainable, though a pattern of missed payments or an unsatisfied judgment will push the case towards specialist lenders.

How quickly can a director-led bridging loan complete?
Straightforward cases typically complete in 10 to 21 working days, while cases involving development drawdowns or complex company structures can take 4-6 weeks.

Do I need a personal guarantee if I borrow through my limited company?
Often yes, particularly for commercial or investment purchases made through the company, regardless of the company's own trading strength.

What counts as an acceptable exit route for a director applicant?
A mortgage in principle for refinance, estate agent marketing evidence for a sale, or a clear, accountant-confirmed repayment source from company funds are all considered acceptable.

Are interest rates higher for company directors than for PAYE applicants?
Not necessarily. Pricing is driven more by loan-to-value, security type and exit strength than by employment status, though complex structures can add to legal and underwriting costs.

If you are ready to move forward, you can get a bridging loan quote with a broker who understands director income. For a wider view of the options available beyond bridging, our funding solutions hub covers the full range of short-term and commercial finance products we arrange.

title: Bridging Loans for Ground-Up Development: When to Use One
excerpt: A bridging loan for ground up development lets you secure land or a site before planning is granted, then move into full development finance once permission is in place.
metaTitle: Bridging Loans for Ground-Up Development: When to Use One
metaDescription: How a bridging loan for ground up development works, when to use it instead of development finance, real costs, lender criteria and common mistakes UK developers make.
keywords: developer finance, development finance, short-term property finance, site acquisition finance, planning gain finance, bridging loans for developers, pre-planning bridging loan, exit to development finance
author: Mark Higgins
content:
A bridging loan for ground up development buys or secures a site before planning permission is granted, or before full development finance can be arranged. It gives developers speed and certainty at exchange, with refinancing onto a development finance facility once permission is confirmed and the build is ready to start.

We arrange this type of funding constantly, and the pattern never varies. A developer finds a site with strong potential, but the deal moves faster than the planning process or the development lender's paperwork. That is where a bridging loan earns its keep.

Speed is the whole point. Development finance underwriting takes six to eight weeks even on straightforward schemes, and that assumes planning is already in place. A vendor selling at auction or under pressure from their own lender will not wait that long. A bridging loan closes that gap and lets the developer secure the asset while everything else catches up. If you want the fundamentals first, our guide to what bridging finance actually covers is a useful starting point.

What this means in practice

Ground up development almost never starts with a development loan. It starts with a bridging loan that buys time, buys the site, or buys certainty.

Development lenders require planning permission, a fixed-price build contract, a professional team in place and a viable exit before they will release funds for construction costs. Most site acquisitions do not arrive in that state. Vendors want quick, unconditional completion. Auctions demand funds in 28 days. Options and conditional contracts expire before planning is decided.

A bridging loan fills that gap. It funds the purchase now, against the value of the land or existing building, while the planning application progresses in the background. Once consent is granted, the developer refinances onto a development finance facility that funds the actual build.

This is genuinely a two-stage strategy, not a shortcut. Treating it as a shortcut is where developers come unstuck, and we will come back to that.

We see this most often with sites bought at auction, where the legal pack shows an obvious redevelopment opportunity but no planning history. Buyers who assume they can sort finance later, once the hammer falls, find their options have narrowed considerably. Arranging the bridge before bidding, with a lender already comfortable with the site, puts a developer in a far stronger position on the day. This applies equally to sites in major regional markets, from bridging loans in Birmingham to smaller regional centres where auction activity is picking up.

How it works

The mechanics are straightforward. A bridging lender secures against the site or property as it stands today, typically at 60-70% loan to value depending on location and asset type, and releases funds quickly, often within two to four weeks.

The loan runs for a fixed term, usually 6 to 18 months, with interest either serviced monthly or rolled up and repaid at the end. Rolled-up interest is far more common on ground up development bridging loans, since the site generates no income and the developer does not want monthly payments affecting working capital during the planning stage.

Rates on this type of short-term property finance typically sit between 0.85% and 1.25% per month, depending on the strength of the site, the loan to value and how credible the planning strategy is. A clean site with an experienced developer and a strong planning consultant will price towards the lower end. A speculative purchase with no professional input on planning will sit higher, if a lender agrees to it at all. For a wider view of pricing across the market, see our breakdown of current bridging loan rates in the UK.

Arrangement fees are usually 1.5% to 2% of the loan, with an exit fee sometimes added instead of a higher rate, depending on how the lender structures its return. Check whether the exit fee applies regardless of how the developer exits, as some facilities charge it even on early repayment.

The exit is planned from day one. Either the developer refinances onto a development finance facility once planning is granted and a build contract is signed, or the site is sold on with the benefit of planning consent, which is a legitimate and profitable exit for developers who prefer to trade planning gain rather than build out.

Lenders underwriting the bridge will ask about that exit route before they lend, because a bridging loan with no credible way off is the single biggest red flag in this market. If you are weighing up options at this stage, take the time to get a bridging loan quote before committing to a lender.

Plan for delay as well. Planning committees slip, decisions get deferred, and consultation periods run over. A sensible approach builds in a term with some breathing room, or establishes early on whether the lender will consider an extension if planning takes longer than expected. Most will, provided the application is progressing and there is no fundamental problem with the site.

Typical scenarios

Numbers make this real, so here are two we see regularly.

A developer in the East Midlands identified a former commercial yard with strong potential for six townhouses. No planning permission existed yet, but the vendor wanted a 21-day completion. We arranged a bridging loan of £310,000 against a £520,000 site value, 60% LTV, over a 12-month term with rolled-up interest. Funds completed in 16 working days. Planning was granted in month nine, and the developer refinanced onto a development finance facility to fund the build, exiting the bridge in full.

The total interest cost on that facility came to just under £27,900 over the nine months it was actually drawn, rolled up and repaid at refinance. Against a projected gross development value of around £1.4 million once the six townhouses were built and sold, that cost was comfortably absorbed within the scheme's contingency, and the developer still secured the site on their own terms rather than losing it to a cash buyer.

Separately, a residential buyer in Reading found a bungalow on a large plot suitable for a self-build replacement home, but their mortgage lender would not lend on a property they intended to demolish. A bridging loan of £245,000 against a £410,000 purchase price, 59.7% LTV, over a 9-month term let them complete the purchase, submit planning for the new build, and exit either onto a self-build mortgage or a sale once consent was granted. This is common with bridging loans in Reading, where plot values and rebuild potential often outpace what high street lenders are comfortable with.

Planning was granted in month six, three months ahead of the facility's expiry, giving the buyer time to arrange a self-build mortgage without any pressure to rush the decision or accept a worse rate out of necessity. That kind of margin is exactly what a well-structured term should provide. We see similar patterns with bridging loans in London and the wider commuter belt, where plot scarcity pushes more buyers towards this route.

What lenders look for

Lenders want a clear, believable exit, a realistic valuation of the site as it stands, and evidence that the developer or investor has the experience and capital to see the project through.

Loan to value on pre-planning bridging loans typically sits between 55% and 65% of current market value, not the projected value with planning attached. Lenders are deliberately conservative here because planning is never guaranteed. Timescales from enquiry to funds usually run 2 to 4 weeks for a straightforward site with clean title, longer if there are access issues, overage clauses, or unregistered land to sort out. This pattern holds across the country, whether it is bridging loans in Norwich or larger regional cities.

Acceptable security includes bare land, sites with existing structures, and part-developed schemes. Lenders will always want to see a planning strategy document, even an informal one from a planning consultant, setting out the realistic prospects of consent and the likely timeline. They also want proof of the exit, whether that is a development finance agreement in principle, evidence of comparable sales for planning-consented land, or a signed pre-let or forward sale.

Working with the right team

First-time developers are not automatically excluded, but lenders will look more closely at the wider team. A strong architect, an established planning consultant and a contractor with a track record on similar schemes can go a long way to offsetting limited personal experience. Bringing that team to the table early, before the application even goes in, smooths the whole process considerably.

Personal guarantees are standard on this type of lending, and lenders will also want to understand the developer's exposure elsewhere, particularly if other sites or schemes are already geared. A statement of assets and liabilities, along with a clear track record of previous projects where relevant, helps build the case quickly rather than dragging out underwriting with back and forth requests.

The most common reason we see these applications declined is a weak or vague exit. Developers who assume planning will simply be granted, without a fallback if it is refused, delayed or granted with unexpected conditions, put lenders in a difficult position. Having a genuine plan B, whether that is a reduced scheme, a sale of the site as is, or an alternative use, makes a real difference to how a lender views the whole proposal. It is also worth comparing how different lenders approach this risk, and our roundup of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK is a good place to start.

Working with a broker who understands both the bridging loans and development finance markets matters considerably here. The right lender for the bridge is not always the right lender for the eventual development facility, and structuring the exit properly from the outset avoids a scramble later. That is precisely the sort of coordination we handle day to day at Boxx Commercial Finance.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a bridging loan for ground up development?
It is short-term property finance used to buy or secure a site before planning permission is granted or before a full development finance facility can be arranged, giving developers speed and certainty at exchange.

How much can I borrow against a site with no planning permission?
Loan to value on pre-planning bridging loans typically sits between 55% and 65% of the site's current market value, rather than its projected value once planning is granted.

How quickly can a ground up development bridge complete?
Straightforward sites with clean title usually complete in two to four weeks, though this can take longer where there are access issues, overage clauses or unregistered land involved.

What happens if planning permission is delayed?
Most lenders will consider extending the term provided the application is still progressing and there is no fundamental problem with the site, which is why it is sensible to build in some breathing room from the outset.

How do I exit a bridging loan used for ground up development?
The usual exit is refinancing onto a development finance facility once planning is granted and a build contract is signed, though selling the site on with the benefit of planning consent is also a legitimate exit.

Can first-time developers get this type of funding?
Yes, though lenders will look more closely at the wider team, including the architect, planning consultant and contractor, to offset limited personal development experience.

What rates should I expect on this type of bridging loan?
Rates typically sit between 0.85% and 1.25% per month, depending on the strength of the site, the loan to value and how credible the planning strategy is.

If you are structuring a site purchase and want to talk through the options, our funding solutions team can help you weigh up the bridge and the eventual development exit together. You can also get a bridging loan quote to get the process moving.

title: Why Use a Whole-of-Market Bridging Broker?
excerpt: A whole of market broker searches the entire bridging loans lending panel, not just a handful of names, so you get sharper rates, faster decisions and fewer declines.
metaTitle: Why Use a Whole-of-Market Bridging Broker
metaDescription: Why Use a Whole-of-Market Bridging Broker. Expert advice from Boxx Commercial Finance, a whole-of-market UK bridging finance broker.
keywords: whole of market bridging loans broker, bridging loans broker UK, independent bridging loan broker, compare bridging loan lenders, bridging loans for developers, fast property finance broker, specialist property finance broker
author: Andrew Farrimond
content:
A whole of market bridging loans broker is worth using because they search the entire lending panel, typically 80 to 100+ active lenders, rather than the handful a single institution or tied adviser can offer. Businesses use a whole of market bridging broker approach when speed, price and certainty of completion all matter, because no single lender is consistently best across every deal type, security or exit strategy.

In our experience, most borrowers who go direct to one lender, or rely on a broker tied to a small panel, end up paying more than they needed to, or worse, get declined for reasons that a different lender would have happily accepted. This article addresses that problem directly. If you want to see how this works for your own situation, you can get a bridging loan quote.

Bridging loans move fast, and the lender market moves just as fast underneath it. New funders enter the market, others tighten criteria overnight, and rates shift week to week depending on where each lender sits with their own funding lines. A broker who spends every working day in that market sees these shifts as they happen. A borrower dealing with one bank sees none of it, because they only ever hear what that one lender is prepared to offer. For a fuller explanation of the product itself, see our guide to what bridging finance actually involves.

This matters more than it might first appear. A deal that gets declined by one lender on a Tuesday can often be approved by another lender on the Wednesday, with identical paperwork and identical security. The difference is not the deal, it is which lender you happened to ask.

What this means in practice

In practice, using a whole of market broker means someone else does the legwork of matching your deal to the right lender, rather than you or a single adviser guessing which one might say yes.

Short-term property finance is not a commoditised product. Rates, fees, valuation requirements, acceptable security types and appetite for complex borrowers vary enormously between lenders. A high street bank-owned bridging arm might refuse a deal with unregistered land or a borrower with adverse credit, while a specialist lender three doors down would fund it within days.

A whole of market broker like Boxx Commercial Finance holds relationships across the private lender, challenger bank and institutional funder space. That means when your circumstances are slightly unusual, and in bridging loans, most circumstances are slightly unusual, there is still a realistic route to funding.

The practical difference shows up in three places: the interest rate you pay, the speed of the decision, and whether the deal completes at all. All three matter significantly in bridging loans because the clock is usually running against you.

Rate differences between lenders on the same deal can be surprisingly wide. Quotes ranging from 0.55% to 0.95% per month are not unusual for what is essentially the same risk profile, simply because lenders price their books differently depending on current appetite. Over a nine month bridge on a £400,000 loan, that gap means a difference of over £14,000 in total interest. A broker who knows which lenders are hungry for that type of deal right now can save a genuinely significant sum, not just shave a fraction off the headline rate.

Flexibility on fees also matters. Some lenders will negotiate arrangement fees or waive exit fees for a strong deal, particularly if they are keen to deploy capital that quarter. A broker with an existing relationship and a track record of good quality introductions is far more likely to get that flexibility than a borrower calling in cold.

How it works

The process starts with a short conversation about the security, the exit and the timescale, then the broker runs the deal against live lender criteria rather than a generic checklist.

A good broker will ask pointed questions early: what is the exit route, is there a live sale agreed or a refinance planned, is there planning permission in place if it is a development exit, and what condition is the security property in right now. These answers determine which lenders are even worth approaching.

From there, the broker packages the deal, often with an indicative decision in principle within 24 to 48 hours, and puts it to two or three lenders most likely to say yes on the best terms, rather than scattering the application everywhere. Valuation is instructed, legal work runs in parallel, and funds are released once the solicitor confirms everything is in order.

This is where a broker earns their fee. Approaching lenders one at a time, waiting for a decline, then trying the next, can burn two or three weeks you do not have. A broker who knows the panel cuts straight to the lenders with genuine appetite.

A typical timeline for a straightforward case looks something like this. Day one, initial fact find and decision in principle. Day two to four, application packaged and submitted to shortlisted lenders, valuation instructed. Day five to eight, valuation report back, formal offer issued. Day nine to twelve, legal work completed and funds released. Complex cases involving planning, multiple securities or unregistered land will run longer, but the shape of the process stays the same.

Throughout that process, the broker also acts as a buffer between borrower and lender, chasing solicitors, pushing valuers for quicker turnaround, and flagging any underwriting queries the moment they arise rather than letting them sit in an inbox for three days. That project management role frequently makes the difference between a nine day completion and a nineteen day completion.

Typical scenarios

Two scenarios show how this plays out for the two main types of bridging loans borrower: the residential buyer and the developer.

A homeowner in Reading exchanged on a new property but her buyer pulled out three days before completion. She needed £310,000 against a £480,000 property (65% LTV) over 6 months to complete the purchase without losing the chain, exiting via the eventual resale of her existing home. Because the case had a slightly complex title issue, two of the first lenders approached declined it. A whole of market broker placed it with a specialist lender who understood the title position, and funds released in 9 working days.

A developer near Norwich needed £620,000 against a site valued at £950,000 once refurbished (65% LTV on GDV) over 12 months, to complete a conversion of a former commercial unit into six flats. The exit was a planned refinance onto a term facility once units were let. Because this required staged drawdowns against works completed, only a subset of lenders on the panel offered that structure. The broker matched the deal to one of them and the facility completed in 16 working days, with the first drawdown released a week later.

A third example worth mentioning involves an auction purchase, since these are among the most time sensitive bridging cases we see. A landlord in Birmingham won a semi-commercial lot at auction with a 28 day completion deadline, needing £185,000 against a £260,000 valuation. Mainstream lenders could not move quickly enough given their standard underwriting timescales. A specialist auction-friendly lender on the broker's panel completed within 21 days, comfortably inside the deadline, avoiding the loss of the deposit.

Similar deals happen regularly for landlords needing bridging loans in London, buyers securing auction purchases with bridging loans in Birmingham, and developers running refurbishment projects using bridging loans in Reading. We also regularly place bridging loans in Norwich for developers working on conversion projects like the one above.

What lenders look for

Lenders want a credible exit, adequate security cover and clean title, and they want evidence of all three before they will commit, not just an assurance that it will be fine.

Typical loan-to-value sits between 65% and 75% on standard residential security, dropping to 55% to 65% for land, semi-commercial or unusual assets. Timescales from enquiry to funds vary from 5 working days for a straightforward regulated bridge with clean title, to 3 to 4 weeks where planning, structural issues or complex ownership need resolving.

Acceptable security ranges from residential and commercial property to land with or without planning, though pricing and LTV shift sharply depending on which. Lenders expect evidence of the exit, whether that is a signed sale memorandum, an agreement in principle for the refinance mortgage, or a schedule of works and planning consent for a development exit.

The most common reason we see applications declined is a vague or unsubstantiated exit strategy, followed closely by valuations coming in lower than the borrower expected, which throws the LTV out. Lenders rarely say this outright, but a case presented with a clear, evidenced exit from day one moves through underwriting noticeably faster than one where the broker or borrower has to chase documents mid-application.

Credit history also plays a part, though far less than most borrowers assume. Bridging lenders are generally more concerned with the strength of the security and exit than with a handful of historic missed payments or a County Court Judgment. That said, undischarged bankruptcy or a very recent history of serious arrears will narrow the panel considerably, which is exactly the sort of situation where knowing which lenders still have appetite becomes valuable. Some of the leading UK bridging loan lenders specialise precisely in these harder-to-place cases.

Property type matters too. Standard bricks and mortar residential property attracts the widest lender pool and the sharpest pricing. Flats above commercial premises, properties of non-standard construction, or land without planning will always attract a smaller, more specialist panel, and pricing typically reflects that reduced competition with rates sitting half a point or more above standard cases.

Common mistakes

The biggest mistake is approaching multiple lenders directly at once, which creates duplicate credit searches and can actually slow decisions down rather than speed them up.

Another frequent error is underestimating total cost. Borrowers focus on the headline monthly rate and forget arrangement fees, valuation fees, legal costs and exit fees, which together can add several percentage points to the real cost of the loan. Our current overview of UK bridging loan rates breaks this down in more detail.

We also see borrowers leave the exit strategy too vague, assuming that a sale will happen or a refinance will be approved without having anything in writing to back it up. Lenders want to see a mortgage agreement in principle, a signed memorandum of sale, or a clear schedule of works with planning consent already in place, not just an assumption that everything will fall into place in time.

Timing is another common trap. Borrowers often start the process too late, treating short-term property finance as a last resort rather than planning ahead, which leaves no room for a valuation to come back lower than expected or for a legal query to add a few extra days. Building in a sensible buffer, and speaking to a broker as soon as the need becomes apparent rather than when the deadline is already looming, makes a material difference to how smoothly the whole process runs.

Finally, some borrowers choose the cheapest quoted rate without checking whether that lender can actually deliver within the required timescale. A slightly higher rate from a lender who reliably completes in ten days is almost always better value than the cheapest rate from a lender who might take four weeks, particularly when a chain, an auction deadline or a development drawdown schedule is riding on it. This is precisely the judgement call a whole of market broker is placed to make, weighing price against certainty rather than chasing the lowest number on a rate sheet.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a whole of market bridging broker?
A whole of market bridging broker is a broker who can access the entire bridging lender panel, typically 80 to 100+ active lenders, rather than being tied to a small number of institutions, so they can match a deal to the lender most likely to accept it on the best terms.

Why not just go direct to a bank for a bridging loan?
Going direct limits you to one lender's criteria and pricing. If that lender declines or prices the deal poorly, you have no comparison, whereas a whole of market broker can place the same deal with a different lender who may accept it or offer better terms.

How much can a whole of market broker actually save on a bridging loan?
Rate differences between lenders for the same risk profile can range from 0.55% to 0.95% per month, which on a £400,000 loan over nine months can mean a difference of over £14,000 in total interest.

How quickly can a bridging loan complete with a whole of market broker?
Straightforward cases can complete in as little as 9 to 12 working days from initial enquiry, though complex cases involving planning, multiple securities or unregistered land can take 3 to 4 weeks.

What do lenders look for when assessing a bridging loan application?
Lenders want a credible, evidenced exit strategy, adequate security cover, and clean title. Loan-to-value typically sits between 65% and 75% for standard residential security, dropping to 55% to 65% for land or unusual assets.

Does bad credit stop me getting a bridging loan?
Not usually. Bridging lenders focus more on the strength of the security and exit strategy than on historic credit issues, though undischarged bankruptcy or very recent serious arrears will narrow the available panel.

What is the most common mistake borrowers make with bridging loans?

content:
A second charge bridging loan is a short-term loan secured against a property that already has a mortgage or first charge loan on it, sitting behind the existing lender in priority. Businesses and property owners use it when they need to release equity quickly without remortgaging or disturbing a first mortgage that may have a good rate or early repayment penalties attached.

What this means in practice

In practice, a second charge bridging loan lets you borrow against the equity in a property while your original mortgage stays exactly where it is. The second charge lender takes a legal charge that ranks behind the first lender, meaning if the property were ever sold and the debt called in, the first charge holder gets paid before the second.

This matters because it changes the risk profile for the lender, and therefore the price and terms you're offered. Landlords often use this structure when they have a competitively priced buy-to-let mortgage they want to keep in place, but need £50,000 to £300,000 quickly for another purchase, a refurbishment, or to cover a tax bill.

Developers holding a site with existing development finance in place commonly need a top-up facility to fund an unexpected cost overrun without unwinding the whole capital stack. The key point is that the first charge lender has to agree to it happening at all, which is where a lot of deals either move quickly or stall completely.

How it works

The mechanics start with your existing first charge lender giving formal consent for a second charge to be registered against the title. Without that consent in writing, no second charge lender will proceed.

Once consent is confirmed, the second charge lender values the property, checks the outstanding balance and terms of the first mortgage, and calculates their lending based on the gap between the property's value and the total debt across both charges. Legal work runs in parallel, usually with the borrower's solicitor liaising with both lenders' solicitors to register the charges in the correct order at the Land Registry.

Interest is typically rolled up or retained rather than paid monthly, which keeps affordability checks simpler for the lender since they're not relying on your income to service two separate loans. Exit usually happens via sale of the property, refinance of the whole debt into one facility, or repayment from another source such as the sale of a different asset.

For borrowers weighing this up, it's worth comparing how short-term property finance actually works before assuming a second charge is automatically the right structure, because sometimes a full remortgage or a first charge bridging loan elsewhere in the portfolio works out cheaper overall.

Typical scenarios

Here's a real pattern we see often. A landlord in Reading owned a buy-to-let worth £420,000 with an existing mortgage of £210,000 at a rate fixed until 2027 that they had no intention of breaking. They needed £95,000 to complete a cash purchase of another property before a vendor's deadline.

We arranged a second charge bridging loan of £95,000 against the Reading property, taking total secured debt to £305,000 against the £420,000 valuation, a combined LTV of 72.6%. The term was 10 months, exiting via remortgage of the newly purchased property once refurbishment works were finished and it qualified for standard buy-to-let lending. Funds released in 16 working days from first charge consent being confirmed, which was the main variable affecting timing.

On the developer side, we worked with a small development company in Birmingham part-way through a six-unit scheme, funded by a first charge development loan. An unexpected planning condition added £40,000 to the build cost. Rather than renegotiate the whole facility, we secured a £40,000 second charge bridging loan against the completed value of one nearly-finished unit, over a 6-month term, repaid on the sale of that unit. It completed in 3 weeks, largely because the first charge lender was already familiar with the scheme and consented quickly.

If you're weighing up a similar deal, you can get a bridging loan quote before you approach your first charge lender, so you know what's realistic.

What lenders look for

Lenders assess combined loan-to-value across both charges, the strength of your exit, and how cooperative the first charge lender is likely to be. Most second charge bridging lenders will lend up to 70-75% combined LTV on residential property, sometimes stretching to 80% for very strong exits or prime locations, and typically 65-70% on commercial or semi-commercial property.

Timescales from enquiry to funds usually run 2 to 4 weeks, though we've seen cases complete in under 10 working days when the first charge lender is responsive and the legal work is straightforward. The biggest single variable is how quickly the first charge lender issues formal consent. Some lenders, particularly larger high street banks, can take three weeks just to process that request, so we always chase this the moment an enquiry lands on our desk.

Acceptable security includes residential investment property, semi-commercial units, and development sites with sufficient equity, though lenders are more cautious about second charges on owner-occupied residential property because of additional regulatory requirements under FCA rules. Lenders scrutinise evidence of exit closely, whether that's a signed sale memorandum, a mortgage agreement in principle for the refinance, or a clear build programme with realistic completion dates.

In our experience, the most common reason these applications are declined is not the borrower's credit profile. Instead, the first charge lender refuses or delays consent, or the combined LTV comes out higher than expected once the second charge lender's valuer revises the property's worth downward.

Common mistakes

The biggest mistake is applying for a second charge bridging loan before checking whether the first charge lender will actually consent. We've had deals fall over in week three because nobody asked the question in week one.

Another frequent error is underestimating combined LTV. Borrowers often calculate based on the property's value against just the new loan, forgetting the first mortgage balance is added into the lender's calculation too. This catches people out on properties that have seen limited value growth since purchase.

Borrowers sometimes assume a second charge will be roughly the same price as a first charge bridging loan. It won't be. Second charge lenders price in the subordination risk, so rates typically run 0.5% to 1.5% per month higher than an equivalent first charge deal, and arrangement fees can be marginally higher too. Not factoring this into the overall cost of the exit strategy is a recurring problem we're called in to fix after the fact.

Alternatives or comparisons

A second charge bridging loan is the wrong choice when a straightforward remortgage or further advance from your existing lender would achieve the same result more cheaply. If your first charge lender offers a further advance at a rate close to your existing mortgage, that will almost always beat a second charge bridging loan on cost, and it avoids the consent and dual-legal-fee complexity entirely.

It's also the wrong tool if your first charge lender is known to refuse consent outright, which some are, particularly certain buy-to-let lenders with restrictive terms. In that situation, a first charge bridging loan to fully refinance and replace the existing mortgage is usually the more realistic route, even though it means giving up a good existing rate.

If the amount you need is small relative to the property's equity and speed isn't critical, an unsecured business loan or a personal loan may work out cheaper and faster than the legal process a second charge requires. If you have three months or more before you need funds, it's worth exploring whether standard refinancing beats bridging altogether. This is where checking current UK bridging loan rates against remortgage pricing pays off before committing.

How to get the best outcome

Start by contacting your first charge lender directly, or asking your broker to do it, to confirm they'll consent to a second charge before you spend time on anything else. This single step saves more failed applications than any other piece of advice we give.

Work out your combined LTV honestly and early, using a realistic current valuation rather than what the property was worth when you bought it. Document your exit strategy, whether that's a sale agreement, remortgage AIP, or development completion schedule, because lenders want to see it in writing, not just hear it described.

If you'd like to compare bridging loan rates against a full refinance before deciding which route makes sense for your situation, that conversation is worth having before you approach any lender directly. Boxx Commercial Finance arranges second charge bridging loans across England and Wales and can usually tell you within a day whether your first charge lender is likely to cooperate, based on our experience with them on previous deals.

We also regularly place deals for clients needing a second charge bridging solution where the first charge lender is a well-known high street name, so we usually know their consent process and typical turnaround times in advance, which saves clients weeks of uncertainty. It's often worth comparing lenders first by checking our list of top-rated UK bridging lenders before you commit to one.

Summary

A second charge bridging loan can be a genuinely useful tool when you need to raise funds fast without disturbing a good first mortgage, but it only works smoothly when consent is secured early, combined LTV is realistic, and the exit is solid. Get those three things right and it's often the fastest route to unlocking equity you already own. Get them wrong and you'll lose weeks chasing a deal that was never going to complete.

Whether you're based in London, Birmingham, Norwich or Reading, the fundamentals are the same, though local property values and typical first charge lenders vary by region, which is why we look at each deal individually rather than applying a blanket approach.
