content:
Bridging loans for buy to let are short-term loans that let landlords buy property a mainstream mortgage lender would refuse, usually because it lacks a kitchen or bathroom, has no valid EPC, or is otherwise unmortgageable in its current state. The landlord uses bridging loans for buy to let purchases to complete quickly, carries out the refurbishment, then refinances onto a standard buy to let mortgage once the property meets lending criteria.

We arrange this type of deal constantly at Boxx Commercial Finance, and it remains one of the most reliable strategies in the private rented sector. Auction stock, probate properties and ex-local authority flats in poor condition rarely qualify for a mortgage on day one. Bridging loans exist to close that gap between what a property is worth now and what it will be worth once it's habitable and rentable.

What this means in practice

In practice, this means you can move on a property that ninety per cent of buy to let investors cannot touch, because most of them are relying on mortgage finance that simply won't be approved against a property with no working kitchen or a collapsed ceiling.

You buy with cash-like speed using a bridging loan, secured against the property itself plus sometimes additional security. You then spend weeks or months bringing it up to a lettable, mortgageable standard. Once the work is done and the property has an EPC rating a BTL lender will accept, you refinance onto a term mortgage and repay the bridge in full.

The gap between purchase and refinance is where the profit sits, but it's also where the risk sits. Landlords who plan this properly with a realistic budget and a genuine understanding of local rental demand tend to do very well. Those who go in optimistic about timescales and costs end up ringing us in month eight asking for an extension.

How it works

The mechanics are straightforward once you've done one or two. A short-term property finance lender values the property in its current condition and lends against that, typically between 65% and 75% loan to value depending on the property type and location. Some lenders will also lend against the works cost in stages, releasing funds as the refurbishment progresses.

You draw the loan, complete the purchase, and start work. Interest usually accrues monthly rather than being paid from your own pocket during the term, which matters if the property isn't producing rent yet. Most bridging loans in this space run for six to twelve months, though some landlords request longer if the refurbishment is more substantial or involves planning permission.

Once the property is finished, it's revalued at the higher, post-works figure. A buy to let mortgage lender then assesses it against that new valuation and the achievable rent, and if it stacks up, you refinance and clear the bridge. The uplift in value from the works is usually what makes the whole strategy pay for itself, alongside the rental income you start collecting from that point.

If you'd like to get a bridging loan quote before you commit to a purchase, our team can talk you through current lender criteria and what's realistic for your project.

Typical scenarios

A landlord in Norwich found a two-bed terrace at auction for £110,000. It had no kitchen, damp in one bedroom, and an EPC rating of F, so no mainstream lender would touch it. We arranged a bridging loan of £77,000 against the £110,000 purchase price, a 70% loan to value, over a nine month term. The landlord spent £18,000 on refurbishment, including a new kitchen, damp treatment and insulation to bring the EPC up to C. The property was revalued at £158,000 post-works, and she refinanced onto a five year fixed buy to let mortgage at 75% LTV, clearing the bridge and pulling out most of her deposit. Completion on the bridge itself took eleven working days from application.

A different case involved a small developer converting a former shop with a flat above into two self-contained flats in Birmingham, a project that needed developer finance rather than a standard purchase bridge. We secured £240,000 against a gross development value of £420,000 once converted, staged in three drawdowns tied to build progress, over a twelve month term. Both flats let quickly given strong tenant demand in that part of the city, and the developer refinanced onto BTL mortgages for both units at the end of the build. This shows how bridging loans for buy to let purchases and light development work overlap in practice.

What lenders look for

Lenders want a clear, credible exit above everything else. They will ask exactly how you plan to repay the loan, whether that's a refinance onto a BTL mortgage or a sale, and they'll want evidence it's realistic, not just a plan on paper.

Loan to value on unmortgageable buy to let property typically sits between 65% and 75% of current value, sometimes with an additional facility for works costs released in stages against certified progress. Lenders will want a schedule of works, a realistic costed budget, and ideally a contractor with a track record, particularly on anything involving structural changes.

Timescales from enquiry to funds released usually run seven to fifteen working days for a straightforward case with clean title and no complex legal issues. That stretches significantly if there's an unregistered title, a lease that needs extending, or a property with multiple owners in probate. Security is almost always a first charge over the property, though some lenders will take a second charge behind an existing mortgage if there's sufficient equity.

The most common reason we see applications declined is an unrealistic exit. If a landlord's refinance plan assumes a rental yield or a post-works valuation that the numbers simply don't support, the lender will pick that apart at underwriting stage. We'd rather catch that at the enquiry stage than have a client find out three weeks into a purchase.

Common mistakes

The biggest mistake we see is underestimating the refurbishment timescale. Landlords budget for six weeks of work and it takes fourteen, which means more months of bridging interest eating into the profit than they planned for.

Second is underestimating cost. Materials and labour costs have moved significantly over the last two years, and a budget based on a mate's quote from three years ago is not a budget, it's a guess. Build in a contingency of at least fifteen per cent.

Third, and this trips people up more than they expect, is not checking the exit mortgage criteria before starting work. Some BTL lenders won't lend on certain property types, or require specific minimum floor areas, or won't accept a particular type of ex-local authority build. Check this before you buy, not after the refurbishment is finished.

Fourth, some landlords assume they can extend the bridge indefinitely if the refinance takes longer than expected. Extensions are possible but not guaranteed, and they come at a cost. Lenders rarely say this outright, but a request for a second extension on a loan that's already run over term tends to get far more scrutiny than the original application.

Alternatives or comparisons

Bridging loans are the wrong choice if the property is already mortgageable and you're simply trying to move fast on a straightforward purchase. In that case, a standard buy to let mortgage or a mortgage with a fast-track underwriter is cheaper and there's no need to take on bridging costs at all.

They're also the wrong tool if your refurbishment budget is genuinely uncertain or the property needs planning permission with a real risk of refusal. In that scenario, a bridge with no clear exit is a dangerous position. It's better to secure planning first, using either your own funds or a shorter-term option, before committing to a bridging facility with a fixed repayment clock running.

If you're a developer taking on a heavier scheme involving multiple units, a full development finance facility with drawdowns tied to build stages is usually more appropriate than a standard bridge, since it's structured specifically for that purpose and often works out more cost-effective over a longer build programme.

For landlords deciding between the two, we'd generally point towards bridging loans when the works are cosmetic to moderate and the timeline is under twelve months, and towards development finance when you're looking at conversions, extensions, or new build elements with a longer programme.

How to get the best outcome

Get your numbers stress-tested before you commit to a purchase, not after. A broker who arranges these deals regularly can sanity-check your refurbishment budget, your post-works valuation assumption and your exit rental yield against what lenders are actually approving right now.

If you want to compare bridging loan rates and terms across lenders before you make an offer, talk to us early rather than once you've already exchanged. We can often flag issues with a proposed exit strategy before they become a problem three months into a project.

Have your exit mortgage broker involved from day one too. There's little point refurbishing a property to a standard that one BTL lender likes if another lender, with better rates, has criteria that rules it out. Checking both ends of the deal at the same time avoids expensive surprises. For current market context, it's worth reviewing current UK bridging loan rates so your cost assumptions are realistic from the outset, and understanding which UK bridging lenders suit refurbishment deals before you approach one directly.

If none of this is familiar territory, our guide on how bridging loans work for property investors is a useful starting point before you explore a specific purchase.

Summary

Bridging loans for buy to let give landlords and developers a way into unmortgageable property that most buyers can't access, provided the refurbishment budget, timeline and exit are all realistic from the start. Get those three things right and the strategy consistently works. Get them wrong and the bridging costs quietly erode what should have been a healthy profit.

We work with landlords across the country on exactly this kind of deal, from first-time investors in Reading to experienced developers running multiple projects, and we'd rather talk through the numbers with you before you commit than help you fix a problem afterwards. acceptedAnswer.text: Not in the same sense. Bridging lenders need a specific, evidenced exit such as a sale or refinance within the term. Secured business loans are repaid through monthly instalments from trading income, so the lender is assessing ongoing affordability rather than a single exit event.

mainEntity.name: What loan-to-value can I expect on each product?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bridging loans typically go up to 70-75% LTV on standard residential property and 60-65% on land or commercial assets. Secured business loans tend to sit at 60-70% LTV, reflecting the longer-term risk a lender takes on when repayment depends on years of trading performance.

mainEntity.name: Can developers use either product for a refurbishment project?

acceptedAnswer.text: Developers most commonly use bridging loans or dedicated developer finance for refurbishment because the funding need is short-term and tied to a specific project timeline. A secured business loan can work if the developer wants to hold the asset long-term rather than sell or refinance quickly.

mainEntity.name: Will a bad credit history rule me out of both products?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bridging lenders focus more heavily on the security property and exit than on personal credit history, so adverse credit is often manageable. Secured business loan lenders weigh personal and business credit more heavily since repayment depends on ongoing trading performance rather than a single sale or refinance.

mainEntity.name: Which product suits a business that just needs working capital?

acceptedAnswer.text: A secured business loan almost always suits working capital needs better than bridging. Bridging is priced and structured for a defined short-term exit, and using it to plug ongoing cashflow gaps without a clear repayment event is one of the more expensive mistakes a business can make.

content:
A bridging loan vs secured business loan decision comes down to speed and purpose. Bridging loans are short-term, fast-completing facilities secured against property, typically used for time-critical purchases, chain breaks or development exits. Secured business loans are longer-term facilities, usually repaid over one to fifteen years, used to fund working capital, expansion or asset purchase against business or property assets.

We get asked this question most weeks, usually by a client who has been quoted both products by different brokers and cannot work out why the pricing looks so different. The honest answer is that they are not really competing products. They solve different problems, and picking the wrong one costs you money and, sometimes, the deal itself. If you'd rather talk it through than read on, you can get a bridging loan quote with our team directly.

Think of them as sitting at different points on a timeline rather than as rivals for the same job. Bridging is designed to get you from one fixed point to another, quickly and at a cost that reflects urgency. A secured business loan is designed to sit quietly in the background of a business for years, funding growth without demanding attention every few months. Once clients see it that way, the rest of the decision usually falls into place fairly naturally. For a fuller grounding in the basics, our guide on what bridging finance actually covers is a useful starting point.

What this means in practice

In practice, the choice usually reveals itself once you are honest about your timeline and your exit. If you need funds in under three weeks, or you are buying something a mainstream lender would call unmortgageable, you are almost certainly looking at bridging loans in London, Birmingham or anywhere else in the UK.

Secured business loans suit a different profile entirely. They work well when a business needs a lump sum against property or fixed assets, but has time to go through a fuller underwriting process and wants a predictable monthly repayment over several years rather than a lump-sum exit.

The mistake we see most often is a business owner assuming the two products are interchangeable because both involve a charge over property. They are not. A bridging loan is priced monthly because it is meant to be short-lived. A secured business loan is priced annually because it is meant to run for years. Comparing the headline rate of one against the other without adjusting for term length gives a completely misleading picture of true cost.

To put that in real terms, a bridging loan at 0.85% per month works out at roughly 10.2% a year before fees, which sounds expensive next to a secured business loan advertised at 9% per annum. But over a three-month bridge, the actual interest cost might be around £3,570 on a £140,000 loan, whereas the same sum tied up for three years on a secured loan, even at a lower headline rate, would cost considerably more in total interest once you add in the extra time on risk. Rate alone tells you very little until you multiply it by the term you actually need. Our breakdown of current UK bridging loan rates goes into this comparison in more detail.

We also see clients get caught out by fees rather than rate. Bridging loans typically carry an arrangement fee of 1-2%, a valuation fee, and sometimes an exit fee, all of which need factoring into the real cost of borrowing over a short period. Secured business loans usually carry a smaller arrangement fee proportionally, because that cost is spread across a much longer term. Neither is wrong, but the fee structure only makes sense once you know how long the money is actually working for you.

How it works

Both products are secured, meaning a lender takes a legal charge over property or another qualifying asset, but the mechanics of underwriting and repayment differ sharply.

A bridging loan is underwritten primarily against the value of the security property and the credibility of your exit plan. Lenders care less about your business's trading history and more about whether the property will sell or refinance within the agreed term. Interest is usually rolled up or retained, so there is no monthly outgoing during the loan, which suits property transactions where cashflow is tied up until completion or sale.

Rolled-up interest means the lender adds the interest to the loan balance and takes it all at redemption, while retained interest means several months are deducted from the gross loan at the outset and held by the lender. Both achieve the same outcome: no monthly payment for the borrower. They do, however, affect how much cash actually lands in your account on day one. Ask a lender to show both figures side by side before signing anything.

A secured business loan is underwritten more like a traditional commercial mortgage. Lenders look at business turnover, profitability, bank statements and sometimes personal guarantees, alongside the security offered. Repayments are amortised monthly across the term, so affordability testing on ongoing income matters far more than it does with bridging.

Because affordability is central to a secured business loan, lenders will typically ask for the last two to three years of filed accounts, six to twelve months of business bank statements, and a breakdown of existing debt commitments. Where a business has seasonal income, such as agriculture or hospitality, some lenders will build in repayment holidays or stepped payments to reflect cashflow patterns rather than insisting on a flat monthly figure all year round.

The two products overlap in speed of legal work. Both require a solicitor to register a charge, and both benefit from having title deeds and any existing charges sorted out early. We have found that development finance clients moving between short-term property finance and a longer-term facility save real time if their solicitor is briefed on both possibilities from day one.

One practical step that speeds up either route is instructing a solicitor who is already familiar with the specific lender's standard documentation. Many bridging lenders and secured loan providers work from a panel of firms who know their paperwork inside out, and using a solicitor outside that panel can add a week or more simply through unfamiliarity with the requirements. It is a small detail that clients rarely think to ask about, but it consistently makes a measurable difference to completion dates.

Typical scenarios

Numbers make this easier to picture than theory does, so here are two real shapes of deal we arrange regularly.

A residential investor in Reading found a three-bed terrace at auction, structurally sound but with no working kitchen or bathroom, meaning no high-street mortgage lender would touch it. She needed £142,000 against a purchase price of £210,000 (68% LTV) over a 9-month term, exiting via remortgage once the refurbishment was complete and the property was let. Funds released in 11 working days, ahead of the 28-day auction completion deadline. A secured business loan would never have completed in time. Investors in this position, including those arranging bridging loans in Reading, typically need a lender comfortable with unmortgageable property.

Her total cost on that bridge, including a 1.5% arrangement fee, valuation, and rolled-up interest at 0.79% a month, worked out at just under £13,800 over the nine months. Against that, the property gained an estimated £35,000 in value once refurbished and let, and she refinanced onto a standard buy-to-let mortgage at 68% LTV within the agreed term. The bridge cost money, but it made a deal possible that otherwise would not have existed at all.

Contrast that with a small manufacturing business in Norwich that owned its freehold premises outright and wanted £250,000 to buy a second unit and fund new machinery. There was no urgency and no property sale to exit into. We arranged a secured business loan against the existing freehold, 65% LTV, over a 10-year term with monthly repayments, completing in five weeks after a fuller review of trading accounts. Bridging would have been the wrong tool here, since there was no short-term exit and rolled-up interest over ten years would have been ruinous. Businesses weighing up bridging loans in Norwich against a longer-term facility should look closely at whether a property sale is genuinely on the horizon.

That secured loan completed at 8.9% per annum, giving monthly repayments of roughly £3,150 on the £250,000 advance. Spread over ten years, that gave the business predictable overheads it could plan against, rather than a looming redemption date. The director's view, and one we hear often, was that he would rather know exactly what leaves the account each month than gamble on a sale or refinance materialising on schedule.

What lenders look for

Lenders assess these two products against almost entirely different criteria, and knowing which one they will apply saves wasted applications.

For bridging loans, most lenders will go up to 70-75% LTV on standard residential property and closer to 60-65% on land, commercial or specialist assets. Timescales from enquiry to funds typically run 7 to 21 working days, though we have completed in as little as 5 days when a client already had valuation and legal work in hand. Lenders want a clear, evidenced exit, either a sale with an agreed buyer, a refinance with an agreement in principle, or a development completion certificate. Acceptable security includes residential, semi-commercial, commercial property, and sometimes land with planning potential, which matters for developer finance clients.

Rates on bridging loans currently sit broadly between 0.7% and 1.25% per month depending on LTV, property type and the strength of the exit, with first charge loans generally priced lower than second charge. Lenders will also look closely at whether the exit relies on a single event, such as one buyer, or a broader strategy such as multiple potential refinance lenders, since the latter is seen as materially less risky and is often priced accordingly. For a closer look at how different lenders compare on this, see our review of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK.

For secured business loans, LTVs tend to sit slightly lower, often 60-70%, because the lender is taking a longer-term risk view. Timescales from enquiry to funds usually run 3 to 6 weeks. Lenders expect two to three years of accounts, management information if accounts are dated, and often a personal guarantee from directors. The most common reason we see secured business loan applications declined is inconsistent or unverifiable turnover, particularly with businesses that have grown quickly but cannot yet evidence it on filed accounts.

Interest rates on secured business loans generally range from around 7.5% to 12% per annum depending on the lender, the strength of accounts, and whether the facility is first or second charge against the property. Some lenders will also offer interest-only periods at the start of the term, typically 6 to 12 months, to help a business manage cashflow while a new asset or unit becomes productive. Ask about this option even if it is not advertised, since not every lender volunteers it upfront.

On bridging, the most common decline reason is not the property, but a weak or unevidenced exit. Lenders rarely say this outright, but an application with a vague repayment plan, such as "I'll probably sell it" without a marketing history or agent valuation to back it up, will usually be declined or referred back for more information rather than approved outright. Bringing an agent's valuation, a mortgage agreement in principle, or a build schedule with a completion date to the initial conversation makes a material difference to how quickly a bridging application moves through underwriting. Businesses in the Midlands considering bridging loans in Birmingham should have this evidence ready before the first lender conversation.

Making the right choice for your situation

Ultimately, the right product depends on how quickly you need funds and how you plan to repay them. If you are still unsure after weighing up timelines, exit routes and cost, it is often quicker to talk it through with a broker who can model both options against your actual numbers rather than relying on headline rates alone.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a bridging loan more expensive than a secured business loan?
On a headline monthly rate, bridging looks more expensive, but it is designed to run for a few months rather than years. Once you compare the actual cost over the term you need, a bridging loan is often cheaper for short-term needs, while a secured business loan is cheaper for anything running beyond 12-18 months.

How quickly can I get a bridging loan compared to a secured business loan?
Bridging loans typically complete in 7 to 21 working days, sometimes faster with valuation and legal work already in hand. Secured business loans usually take 3 to 6 weeks because they involve a fuller review of trading accounts and affordability.

Can I use a secured business loan for a property purchase instead of bridging?
Only if the property is mortgageable and there is no time pressure, since secured business loans go through a fuller underwriting process. For unmortgageable property or tight completion deadlines, bridging is almost always the right tool.

What LTV can I expect on each product?
Bridging loans typically go up to 70-75% LTV on residential property and 60-65% on land or commercial assets. Secured business loans tend to sit lower, often 60-70%, reflecting the longer-term risk the lender is taking on.

Do I need an exit strategy for a secured business loan the way I do for bridging?
Not in the same way. Bridging lenders need a clear, evidenced exit such as a sale or refinance, whereas secured business loans are repaid through ongoing trading income via monthly instalments over the term.

Why do bridging loan applications get declined more often than secured business loans?
The most common reason is a weak or unevidenced exit plan, such as an assumed sale with no agent valuation or marketing history behind it. Secured business loan declines are usually down to inconsistent or unverifiable turnover instead.

Which product suits a business buying a second property with no urgency?
A secured business loan is usually the better fit, since there is time for a fuller underwriting process and the business can benefit from predictable monthly repayments over several years rather than a short-term exit.

Every deal is different, and the numbers above are illustrative rather than a quote for your specific situation. If you are weighing up these two routes for a live purchase or funding need, it is worth exploring the full range of funding solutions available, or you can arrange bridging loan vs secured business loan today to see how the figures stack up against your actual timeline and exit.

title: Bridging Loan vs. Development Finance: Which Do You Need?
excerpt: Bridging loans suit quick purchases and light refurbishment funded as one lump sum, while development finance is built for ground-up builds and major works drawn down in stages.
metaTitle: Bridging Loan vs. Development Finance: Which Do You Need?
metaDescription: Bridging loan vs development finance explained by a UK broker: lump sum versus staged drawdown, when to use each, real figures and lender criteria.
keywords: bridging loans vs development finance, developer finance UK, short-term property finance, light refurbishment bridging loan, staged drawdown development finance, bridging loan for property developers, development exit finance
author: Mark Higgins

mainEntity.name: What is the main difference between a bridging loan and development finance?

acceptedAnswer.text: A bridging loan releases the full amount as a single lump sum against the property's current condition, used for quick purchases or light refurbishment. Development finance releases funds in stages as a build progresses, checked by a monitoring surveyor, and is used for ground-up builds or major structural works.

mainEntity.name: Can I use a bridging loan for a small property development?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if the works are light, such as a new kitchen, bathroom, rewire or cosmetic refurbishment. If the project involves structural changes, extensions or a change of use requiring staged building control sign-off, development finance is almost always the better fit and lenders will expect it.

mainEntity.name: Which is cheaper, bridging loans or development finance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Neither is universally cheaper. Bridging loans often carry a lower headline rate but you pay interest on the full amount from day one. Development finance can look pricier per month but interest usually rolls up only on funds actually drawn, which often works out cheaper over a long build.

mainEntity.name: How quickly can a bridging loan complete compared to development finance?

acceptedAnswer.text: A straightforward bridging loan can complete in 2 to 4 weeks, sometimes faster with a specialist lender. Development finance typically takes 4 to 6 weeks to first drawdown due to the additional due diligence around planning, build costs and appointing a monitoring surveyor.

mainEntity.name: Do I need planning permission before applying for development finance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most development finance lenders want planning permission already granted before they'll lend, since it removes a major risk from the project. Some will consider funding at pre-planning stage, but pricing is higher and the pool of lenders willing to do so is much smaller.

mainEntity.name: What happens if my development project overruns and needs more time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most development finance facilities include a mechanism for extending the term, usually at a slightly higher rate, provided the lender is satisfied the project remains viable. It's far cheaper to agree this early with your lender than to reach the end of term with no plan, which is a common and avoidable mistake.

mainEntity.name: Is a bridging loan or development finance better for a first-time developer?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on project scale rather than experience alone, but first-time developers taking on large structural schemes are usually steered toward development finance with an experienced project manager or contractor named on the facility, since lenders want reassurance the build will be delivered competently.

content:
The bridging loan vs development finance decision comes down to one question: are you buying or lightly refurbishing a property with a fixed lump sum, or funding a build that needs money released in stages as work progresses? Bridging loans suit quick completions and cosmetic works. Development finance suits ground-up builds, conversions and heavy structural projects where costs are staged. If you're weighing up your options, you can get a bridging loan quote before deciding which route fits your project.

What this means in practice

In practice, the split isn't about how much you're borrowing, it's about how the money leaves the lender's account and what condition the property is in when you buy it.

A bridging loan hands you the full amount on day one, secured against the property as it stands. You might use it to buy a house at auction, break a chain, or fund light cosmetic refurbishment before selling or refinancing. The works involved are usually the kind you could complete in a few weeks: a new kitchen, redecoration, fixing damp, tidying up a garden. Nothing that needs building control sign-off at multiple stages. For a fuller breakdown of how these facilities work, see our guide on what bridging finance actually covers.

Development finance works completely differently. The lender releases money in tranches as the build hits agreed milestones, checked by a monitoring surveyor. This suits ground-up new builds, loft conversions requiring structural alterations, HMO conversions with significant layout changes, or anything where the works genuinely change the footprint or structure of the building.

We see a lot of borrowers try to force a bridging loan onto a project that's really development finance because the rate looks cheaper on paper. It rarely ends well, and we'll get into why later.

There's also a middle ground that catches people out: the heavier refurbishment bridge. Say you're stripping a property back to add an extra bedroom, knocking through a wall that isn't load-bearing, or converting a garage into living space without altering the footprint much. Some bridging lenders will still fund this under a light or medium refurbishment product, provided the works don't need staged monitoring. The line gets blurry, which is exactly why speaking to a broker before you apply saves a lot of wasted time. We've helped arrange bridging loans in London, bridging loans in Birmingham, bridging loans in Norwich and bridging loans in Reading, and the same principles apply wherever the property sits.

How it works

The mechanics differ at every stage, from how the loan is sized to how funds are released and repaid.

With a bridging loan, the lender values the property in its current state (day-one value) and sometimes also the value after light works (GDV for refurb bridges). You draw the full facility in one go, typically within 2 to 4 weeks of a clean application. Interest is usually rolled up or retained, meaning you don't make monthly payments, it's added to the balance and settled at the end. Terms run from 1 to 18 months, though most bridging loans in our pipeline complete within 6 to 9 months.

Development finance is sized against both the site cost and the build cost, with the loan calculated as a percentage of gross development value (GDV), often 60-70%. Funds are drawn in stages, typically 4 to 6 tranches, released only after a monitoring surveyor confirms the previous stage is complete. Interest usually rolls up on the drawn amount rather than the full facility, which keeps costs down during the early months when less money is out. Terms typically run 12 to 24 months depending on the scale of the build.

Both products exit in the same three ways: sale of the finished asset, refinance onto a term mortgage or buy-to-let product, or repayment from other funds. Lenders on both sides will want to see that exit clearly evidenced before they lend a penny.

One practical difference worth flagging is how each product handles cost overruns. On a bridging loan, if works cost more than expected, you're generally funding that shortfall yourself, since the facility was fixed at outset. On development finance, a contingency line is usually built into the facility from day one, and if that's exhausted, some lenders will consider a further advance, though it's never guaranteed and it slows the build down while it's arranged.

Arrangement fees also differ in how they're structured. Bridging loans typically charge a fee of 1-2% of the gross loan, taken at completion or added to the balance. Development finance fees can be similar at the outset, but there's often an additional exit fee, sometimes 1% of GDV, charged when the facility is repaid. It sounds like a small detail, but on a £2 million GDV scheme that's £20,000 you need to factor into your numbers from the start.

Typical scenarios

Numbers make this far clearer than theory, so here are two recent examples from our own pipeline.

A landlord in Leeds needed £180,000 against a £320,000 buy-to-let property (56% LTV) over 9 months. The property needed a new kitchen, bathroom and rewire, nothing structural. We placed this as a light refurbishment bridging loan, funds released as a single lump sum, exiting via refinance onto a standard buy-to-let mortgage once the works were done and a tenant in place. Completion took 11 working days from instruction.

Compare that with a developer we worked with in the Midlands converting a disused office block into eight flats. Total costs were £1.4 million against a GDV of £2.1 million (67% loan to GDV). We arranged development finance with funds released across five stages, each tied to sign-off from the monitoring surveyor, over an 18-month term. The exit was a mix of unit sales and a small portfolio refinance for the units the developer chose to retain. From first enquiry to first drawdown took just under 6 weeks, largely because of the additional due diligence around planning and build costings.

Both borrowers needed short-term property finance. Neither product would have worked for the other's project.

A third example sits somewhere in between and is worth mentioning because it's increasingly common. A client in Manchester bought a semi-detached property for £240,000 with the intention of adding a two-storey side extension and converting the loft, pushing the end value to around £420,000. Because the extension involved structural steels and a full loft conversion with dormer, this wasn't cosmetic work by any stretch. We placed it as a development finance facility rather than a bridge, with funds released in four stages over 14 months, even though the scale was smaller than a typical ground-up scheme. The lesson here is that scale doesn't decide the product, the nature of the works does. If you're weighing up a similar project, you can speak to a broker and talk through the specifics.

What lenders look for

Lenders assess bridging loans and development finance against very different checklists, even though both sit under the broader specialist property finance umbrella.

For bridging loans, expect loan-to-value up to 75% on standard residential security, sometimes 65-70% on commercial or semi-commercial property. Lenders want a clear, credible exit, usually either a sale agreed or under offer, or a refinance with an agreement in principle already in place. Security can be residential, commercial, mixed-use or land with planning. Timescales from full application to funds run 2 to 4 weeks with a straightforward case, faster if you use a specialist bridging lender with in-house legal. The most common reason we see bridging applications declined is a weak or unevidenced exit, the lender simply isn't convinced the borrower can repay within the term.

For development finance, lenders look at loan to cost (usually up to 90-95% of build costs) and loan to GDV (typically capped at 60-70%). They require a detailed appraisal, a fixed-price build contract or at least a thorough schedule of costs, planning permission already granted, and a monitoring surveyor appointed before drawdown one. Developer experience matters hugely here. Lenders rarely say this outright, but a first-time developer applying for a £1 million-plus facility with no track record will almost always be asked for either a more experienced project manager on board or a personal guarantee backed by tangible assets. Declines here most often come down to unrealistic build costings or insufficient contingency, we always push clients to build in at least 10% contingency before submitting.

It's also worth knowing that both products require a solicitor experienced in specialist finance, not just any high street conveyancer. Development finance in particular involves drafting and reviewing the building contract, collateral warranties, and sometimes an appointment of a project monitor agreement. Using a solicitor unfamiliar with these documents is one of the most common causes of delay we see, often adding two to three weeks to a transaction that should have completed in half that time.

Credit history matters for both products, but lenders take a more forgiving view on bridging loans provided the exit is strong, since the loan is short and asset-backed. Development finance lenders dig deeper, partly because the loan runs longer and partly because they're relying on the developer to manage a live construction site, contractors, and a budget over many months. A poor credit history combined with limited development experience is one of the hardest combinations to place, though not impossible with the right lender and enough compensating factors.

Common mistakes

The single biggest mistake is choosing the product based on rate rather than structure, which almost always costs more in the end.

Borrowers see bridging loan rates advertised from around 0.55% to 0.85% per month and assume that's automatically cheaper than development finance. But if your project genuinely needs staged funding for a structural build, forcing it into a bridging loan means drawing the full amount upfront and paying interest on money sitting unused while the build catches up. You can review our detailed look at current UK bridging loan rates to see how pricing compares across lenders before assuming one product beats the other on cost alone.

Another frequent error is underestimating what counts as structural work in the eyes of a lender. Borrowers often assume that because they're not extending the footprint, the works must be light. But knocking through a load-bearing wall, underpinning, or altering the roof structure will usually tip a project into development finance territory regardless of how modest the budget looks. It's always worth getting a lender's view early, before you've committed to a build contract or exchanged on a purchase.

A third common mistake is failing to line up the monitoring surveyor early enough on a development deal. Lenders won't release the first tranche until the surveyor has reviewed the site and signed off the drawdown request, and if that appointment happens late, it can hold up the entire start of the build. We always recommend getting the monitoring surveyor instructed alongside the legal work, not after it, so there's no gap between practical completion of stage one and the funds landing to pay for stage two.

Finally, some borrowers underestimate how much documentation development finance requires compared with a bridge. Beyond the build contract and planning permission, lenders typically want a detailed cash flow forecast, evidence of professional indemnity insurance for the architect and contractor, and confirmation of warranties such as NHBC or a structural defects policy on residential schemes. Pulling this together after you've applied slows everything down. Getting it ready in advance, ideally with a broker checking the pack before submission, is usually what separates a six-week completion from a three-month one. It's also worth comparing options across the best bridging loan lenders in the UK so you know which lenders are best placed for your type of project.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the main difference between a bridging loan and development finance?
A bridging loan releases the full loan amount upfront against a property's existing value, while development finance is drawn in stages as a build progresses, with each tranche checked off by a monitoring surveyor.

Can I use a bridging loan for a structural renovation?
Generally no. If the works involve structural changes, such as removing load-bearing walls or altering the roofline, lenders will usually require development finance rather than a standard bridging loan.

How quickly can a bridging loan complete compared with development finance?
A straightforward bridging loan can complete in 2 to 4 weeks, sometimes faster with a specialist lender. Development finance typically takes longer, often around 6 weeks, due to additional due diligence on planning and build costs.

Do bridging loans and development finance charge different fees?
Yes. Bridging loans usually charge a 1-2% arrangement fee on the gross loan, while development finance often includes a similar arrangement fee plus an additional exit fee, sometimes around 1% of GDV.

What loan-to-value can I expect on each product?
Bridging loans typically go up to 75% loan-to-value on residential security. Development finance is usually assessed on loan-to-cost (up to 90-95%) and loan-to-GDV (typically capped at 60-70%).

Is my credit history checked the same way for both products?
No. Lenders tend to take a more forgiving view on bridging loans provided the exit is strong, whereas development finance lenders scrutinise credit history more closely given the longer term and construction risk involved.

How do I decide which product is right for my project?
It comes down to the nature of the works rather than the loan size. Cosmetic or light refurbishment projects usually suit a bridging loan, while structural or ground-up builds need development finance. Speaking to a broker early helps avoid costly missteps. You can request a bridging loan quote to get tailored guidance for your project.

For a wider view of the funding options available beyond bridging and development finance, visit our funding solutions hub, or talk to a bridging loan broker to discuss your specific project today.

title: FCA-Regulated Bridging Loans: Consumer Protections
excerpt: FCA regulated bridging loans protect consumers borrowing against their home, with extra checks and safeguards that unregulated business loans don't carry. Here's what UK borrowers need to know.
metaTitle: FCA-Regulated Bridging Loans: Consumer Protections
metaDescription: FCA-Regulated Bridging Loans: Consumer Protections. Expert advice from Boxx Commercial Finance, a whole-of-market UK bridging finance broker.
keywords: regulated bridging loans UK, consumer bridging loan, FCA regulated bridging finance, bridging loan for residential property, unregulated bridging loans, short-term property finance, bridging loan rates UK
author: Andrew Farrimond
content:
FCA regulated bridging loans consumer lending applies whenever a bridging loan is secured against a property that you or an immediate family member lives in, or intends to live in. In that situation, get a bridging loan quote comes with mandatory affordability checks, a right to cancel, and access to the Financial Ombudsman Service if things go wrong. If you'd like to talk through your situation, you can get a bridging loan quote with a member of our team.

Most bridging loans arranged in the UK are actually unregulated, because lenders issue them to limited companies, landlords buying investment property, or developers. The moment your own home becomes the security, or the money is being used to buy a home you'll live in, the rules change entirely. Getting this wrong at application stage is one of the most common reasons deals stall or fail late in the process. Our guide to how bridging finance works covers the basics if you're new to this type of lending.

We see this confusion occur regularly. A client will assume that because they've bought property before, or because they run a small portfolio, the same lending process will apply this time. It may not. The regulatory status of a loan depends on what the property is used for and who lives in it, not on the borrower's experience or track record. Getting a clear answer on this early saves weeks further down the line.

What this means in practice

In practice, regulation determines which lenders you can approach, how quickly they can move, and what paperwork they'll insist on before releasing funds. It isn't a badge of quality; it's a legal category.

A regulated bridging loan means the lender is authorised and supervised by the Financial Conduct Authority specifically for this type of lending and must follow the Mortgage Conduct of Business rules (MCOB). That means proper affordability assessment, clear pre-contract disclosure documents, and a cooling-off period in some cases. The lender also has to demonstrate the loan is suitable, not just that you can technically repay it.

Unregulated bridging, by contrast, operates under contract law rather than consumer protection law. It moves faster because the checks are lighter, but you lose the Ombudsman route if a dispute arises. In our experience, clients are sometimes surprised to learn their loan is unregulated even though it's secured on land next to their house, simply because there's no residential occupation involved. Occupation intent, not property type, determines the outcome.

There's also a practical funding point worth flagging. Not every lender on our panel offers regulated bridging at all. Some deliberately stay out of the space because of the compliance overhead, focusing instead on commercial and investment bridging where turnaround speed is the main selling point. That narrows your options considerably if your loan needs to be regulated, and it's why early identification of the correct category matters so much.

We've had cases where a borrower approached a lender directly, only for the application to stall three weeks in once the lender realised the security property was actually the applicant's residence rather than a buy-to-let. By that point valuation fees had been paid and legal work had started, all of which had to be unwound and restarted with a properly authorised regulated lender. A five minute conversation at the outset would have avoided that entirely.

How it works

The mechanics of a regulated bridging loan follow the same broad shape as any short-term property finance, but with extra steps built in for consumer protection. You apply, a valuation is instructed, the lender assesses your exit route, and funds are released against a legal charge.

Where it differs is in the run-up to offer. A regulated lender must issue a European Standardised Information Sheet or equivalent illustration, confirm your ability to repay through proper income and expenditure checks, and, in many cases, insist you take independent legal advice separate from the lender's own solicitor. Some regulated bridging loans also carry a statutory right of withdrawal, typically 14 days, though most consumers waive this if speed matters, which it usually does.

Interest is almost always rolled up or retained rather than paid monthly, particularly where the loan is funding a chain break or auction purchase and the borrower has no spare income to service payments during the term. Rates for regulated consumer bridging tend to sit a little higher than commercial bridging, reflecting the additional compliance burden lenders carry. You can see current benchmark pricing in our piece on current UK bridging loan rates, though regulated products often price at the upper end of that range.

To put figures on this, regulated bridging typically runs somewhere between 0.55% and 0.95% per month depending on loan-to-value and the lender's own risk appetite. On a £250,000 loan over six months at 0.75% monthly, that's roughly £11,250 in rolled-up interest before fees, which surprises some borrowers who assume bridging pricing is closer to a standard mortgage. Arrangement fees generally sit at 1.5% to 2% of the loan, and there's usually a valuation fee, a broker fee where applicable, and legal costs on both sides to factor in.

Exit fees are less common on regulated products than they used to be, but it's still worth checking the offer document carefully. Some lenders charge an exit fee of 1% if you repay early within the first three months, effectively a minimum interest period. Others charge nothing at all provided you give proper notice. A broker will pick through these details on your behalf, because they rarely get mentioned upfront. If you want a clearer picture of costs for your own circumstances, you can get a bridging loan quote before committing to anything.

Typical scenarios

Two situations dominate regulated bridging enquiries: broken property chains and auction purchases where the buyer will live in the property. Both need speed and both need a lender who can underwrite consumer-grade compliance quickly rather than treating it as an afterthought.

A homeowner in Reading exchanged on a new family house but their buyer pulled out three days before completion. They needed £310,000 against a property valued at £520,000, a loan-to-value of 60%, over a six-month term, exiting via sale of their existing home which was already under offer with a new buyer lined up. Because this was regulated lending secured on a residential chain break, the lender required a full income assessment and a solicitor's undertaking confirming the sale proceeds. Funds completed in 11 working days, tight but workable given the exchange deadline. We arrange similar deals for clients seeking bridging loans in Reading fairly regularly, and chain breaks are consistently the busiest category.

On the developer side, a self-employed buyer in Birmingham bought a run-down terraced house at auction intending to renovate it as her main residence. She needed £145,000 against a £260,000 purchase price, 56% LTV, over nine months, exiting onto a residential mortgage once the refurbishment was complete and she could evidence affordability with a lender. Because she intended to occupy the finished property, this was treated as regulated bridging despite the works involved, and the lender needed a schedule of works alongside the usual income checks. That one took 15 working days from application to completion, slightly longer because of the additional documentation regulated status demands. We see a similar pattern with bridging loans in Birmingham, where auction-driven purchases are a regular feature of enquiries.

A third scenario worth mentioning, less common but not rare, involves inheritance and probate property. A client in Leeds needed to raise £180,000 against a property she'd inherited jointly with her brother, intending to buy out his share and move into the house herself. Because her occupation intent was clear from the outset, the loan was regulated, and the lender wanted evidence of probate progress alongside the standard affordability checks. It completed in 18 working days, longer than average because probate documentation added an extra layer of verification. Clients arranging bridging loans in London and bridging loans in Norwich often raise similar probate-related queries, so this isn't an unusual request.

These cases share a common thread. In every one, the borrower's intention to live in the property, either immediately or once works were complete, is what pulled the loan into regulated territory. The property condition, the loan size, and the term length are secondary to that single question of occupation.

What lenders look for

Regulated bridging lenders look for a credible, evidenced exit and proof you can genuinely afford the loan, not just a plausible story. Loan-to-value typically caps at 70-75% for regulated residential bridging, lower than the 75-80% sometimes seen on unregulated commercial deals.

Timescales from enquiry to funds usually run 10 to 20 working days for regulated cases, longer than unregulated bridging because of the mandatory advice and disclosure steps. Acceptable security is almost always a first charge over residential property, though second charges behind an existing regulated mortgage are possible if the numbers stack up and the first charge lender consents. Lenders want to see a specific, dated exit: an agreed sale, a mortgage offer in principle, or a completion date on a linked purchase. Vague statements like plans to sell at some point or intention to remortgage eventually are rarely enough on their own.

Affordability checks go beyond a simple income multiple. Lenders will examine your existing mortgage commitments, any other secured or unsecured debt, and your general expenditure pattern from bank statements, usually three to six months' worth. For self-employed applicants, expect requests for SA302s or an accountant's certificate covering the last two years, along with business bank statements if the income is drawn irregularly.

Credit history matters too, though not in the same rigid way it does for a standard mortgage. A missed payment two years ago rarely kills an application outright, but recent defaults, unresolved CCJs, or an active IVA will need explaining and may push you toward a smaller panel of specialist lenders who price for that risk. Age can also be a factor on regulated products, since some lenders apply a maximum age at the end of the term, particularly where the exit relies on a future mortgage rather than a sale. Our roundup of the leading bridging loan lenders in the UK gives a sense of how different lenders approach these risk factors.

Property type and condition feed into valuation, and valuers working for regulated lenders tend to be conservative, especially on properties needing renovation before they're mortgageable in the normal sense. A property with no kitchen or bathroom, common with auction purchases, may be valued on both its current condition and its projected value once works are complete, with the loan structured against the lower figure until works progress. A broker who understands how a particular lender's valuation panel thinks can make a genuine difference to how much you're able to borrow.

Finally, most regulated lenders want to see that you've taken, or are arranging to take, independent legal advice separate from their own panel solicitor. This isn't just a box-ticking exercise. It ensures you understand the commitment you're entering into, particularly around what happens if the exit falls through and the loan needs extending or refinancing. A good broker will flag this requirement early so it doesn't become a last-minute delay once everything else is ready to complete.

Costs and fees to budget for

Beyond the headline monthly rate, budget properly for the fees that sit around a regulated bridging loan, since these can add up to a meaningful sum on top of the interest itself. Arrangement fees, valuation costs, legal fees on both sides, and any broker fee should all be factored into your overall borrowing cost before you commit, rather than being treated as an afterthought once the loan is already underway.

Frequently Asked Questions

What makes a bridging loan FCA regulated?
A bridging loan is FCA regulated when it's secured against a property that you or an immediate family member currently lives in, or intends to live in. Occupation intent determines regulatory status, not the loan size, the borrower's experience, or the property type.

Is a regulated bridging loan more expensive than an unregulated one?
Generally, yes. Regulated consumer bridging typically prices at the upper end of the market, between 0.55% and 0.95% per month, reflecting the additional compliance and affordability checks lenders must carry out.

How long does it take to complete a regulated bridging loan?
Most regulated bridging cases take between 10 and 20 working days from enquiry to funds, longer than unregulated bridging because of the mandatory advice, disclosure documents, and affordability assessment involved.

Do I need independent legal advice for a regulated bridging loan?
Most regulated lenders require you to take independent legal advice separate from their own panel solicitor, to ensure you fully understand the commitment before signing, particularly around what happens if the exit route falls through.

What loan-to-value can I get on a regulated bridging loan?
Regulated residential bridging typically caps at 70-75% loan-to-value, slightly lower than the 75-80% sometimes available on unregulated commercial bridging deals.

Can self-employed borrowers get regulated bridging finance?
Yes, though lenders will usually ask for SA302s or an accountant's certificate covering the last two years, alongside business bank statements, to properly assess affordability.

What happens if my exit route falls through on a regulated bridging loan?
Lenders will usually look at extending or refinancing the loan, which is one reason independent legal advice is required upfront, so you understand the implications before the loan completes.

title: Bridging Finance Calculator: Understanding What You'll Pay
excerpt: A bridging loans calculator only tells half the story. Here's how to work out the real cost of a bridging loan once fees, valuation and legal costs are added in.
metaTitle: Bridging Finance Calculator: Understanding What You'll Pay
metaDescription: Use a bridging loans calculator properly with this broker's guide to rate, arrangement fee, exit fee, valuation and legal costs, with worked examples.

content:
A bridging finance calculator gives you a monthly interest figure in seconds, but it rarely shows the full picture. The true cost of a bridging finance calculator for UK businesses should include the interest rate, arrangement fee, exit fee, valuation fee and legal costs together, because those extras can add three to five percent of the loan amount on top of the headline rate. Get this wrong and a deal that looked comfortable on paper will eat far more of your profit than expected.

What this means in practice

A bridging finance calculator serves as a starting point, not a quote. Most online tools ask for the loan amount, term and rate, then produce a monthly interest figure. That works for a quick sanity check, but it won't match what you'll actually pay out at completion or redemption.

The real cost of a short-term property finance deal comprises several separate charges. There's the interest itself, usually charged monthly and either serviced, rolled up or retained. There's an arrangement fee, typically 1.5% to 2% of the loan. There's a valuation fee, which varies depending on the property and how quickly you need the report. There's an exit fee on some products, though not all. And there are legal costs, both your own solicitor's fees and, in most cases, the lender's legal costs too, which you'll be asked to cover.

In our experience, borrowers who only look at the headline rate get caught out. A 0.55% monthly rate sounds cheap until you add a 2% arrangement fee, a £1,200 valuation and £2,500 of combined legal fees on a £250,000 loan. The effective cost then becomes considerably higher than the number the calculator first showed. If you want to understand the basics before running your own numbers, our guide to what bridging finance actually covers is a good starting point.

Most calculators also assume a clean, straightforward case with no delays. In reality, extensions happen. If a sale falls through or a refinance takes longer than expected, you may need to extend the term, and that usually means a further month of interest plus, on some products, an extension fee of around 0.5% to 1%. Build this into your own figures before you commit, rather than discovering it halfway through the term.

A basic calculator won't tell you how the lender treats early repayment. Some bridging loan lenders charge a minimum term of one to three months' interest even if you redeem early, while others allow you to repay at any point without penalty. On a £300,000 loan, the difference between a lender with no minimum term and one with a three-month minimum can easily be £3,000 to £5,000 if your exit comes through faster than planned. Ask this question upfront rather than assume every lender works the same way. If you'd rather talk figures through with someone directly, you can arrange bridging finance calculator today.

How it works

Working out the true cost starts with the loan amount and term, then layers on every fee the lender charges. A basic bridging loan calculation looks like this: monthly interest rate multiplied by the loan amount, multiplied by the number of months, plus the arrangement fee, plus valuation, plus legal costs, plus any exit fee.

Rolled-up interest is added to the loan and repaid at the end, which means you're not finding monthly payments during the term, but the total interest bill is slightly higher because it compounds. Retained interest is deducted from the loan advance upfront, so you receive less money on day one but again avoid monthly payments. Serviced interest means you pay monthly from income, which keeps the total borrowing lower but requires proof of affordability.

Arrangement fees are usually added to the loan rather than paid in cash, so they increase the amount you're borrowing and therefore the interest charged on top. Valuation fees are paid upfront, often before the lender will even issue formal terms. Legal costs are typically settled at completion, and it's worth asking early whether the lender uses a panel solicitor or allows your own, because that affects both cost and speed.

A practical step we always recommend is running the numbers three times: once with the headline rate alone, once with all fees added at the lender's stated figures, and once with an extra month built in as a buffer. This gives you a realistic worst case rather than just a best case. It also puts you in a stronger position when comparing two or three lenders side by side, because the differences in fee structure often matter more than the small gaps in interest rate.

Broker fees are another line item that calculators tend to ignore completely. Where a broker is involved, expect a fee of around 1% of the loan, sometimes charged to the lender rather than the borrower depending on how the deal is structured. Clarify this at the outset, because a good broker will usually save you more in negotiated rate reductions or faster completion than the fee itself costs, but you should still know exactly who is charging what before you sign anything.

If you want a proper worked comparison across lenders before committing, our piece on current UK bridging loan rates breaks down what's typical across the market right now.

Typical scenarios

Numbers make this far clearer than percentages alone. Here are two real patterns we see regularly, one residential and one development-led.

A homeowner in Reading needed to break a chain after their buyer pulled out with exchange three weeks away. They needed £310,000 against a property valued at £520,000 (60% LTV) over a 6-month term, exiting via the sale of their existing home once a new buyer was found. Interest was rolled up at 0.60% a month, the arrangement fee was 2%, valuation came to £950 and legal costs (both sides) totalled £2,800. Total cost of borrowing across the 6 months, including all fees, came to just under £19,400. Funds were released in 9 working days, which meant they didn't lose the onward purchase. Similar chain-break cases are common for clients arranging bridging loans in Reading.

Breaking this down further, the £19,400 comprised roughly £11,160 in rolled-up interest over the six months, £6,200 in arrangement fee, £950 valuation and £2,800 legal costs, with a small variance depending on the exact completion date. Because the loan redeemed in month five rather than running the full six, the borrower actually saved around £1,860 in interest compared with the initial calculator figure, which is a good example of how the calculator gives you a ceiling, not a fixed bill.

A developer in Birmingham needed £480,000 against a semi-derelict commercial building valued at £850,000 post-conversion (56% GDV-based LTV) over 12 months, to fund a light refurbishment and conversion to residential flats. This was developer finance rather than a simple purchase bridge. Interest was retained, arrangement fee was 1.75%, valuation and monitoring surveyor fees came to £2,100, and legal costs were £3,600. The exit was a sale of two of the four completed units, with the other two refinanced onto a term mortgage. Total facility cost across the year worked out at roughly £61,000, and the loan completed in 14 working days from full application. Developers arranging similar deals through bridging loans in Birmingham should expect monitoring surveyor costs to be added where works are involved, which many calculators miss entirely.

On this Birmingham case, the retained interest meant the developer received £480,000 minus roughly £40,300 in interest deducted upfront, so the actual cash available on day one was closer to £439,700. This detail trips up a lot of first-time developers, because a calculator showing a £480,000 loan amount doesn't always make clear that the money in your account will be lower once retained interest is taken off. Always ask the lender for the net advance figure, not just the gross loan amount, before you plan your build costs around it.

A third pattern worth mentioning, though less common, is auction purchase bridging, where speed matters more than rate. A buyer securing a property at auction in Leeds for £195,000 with a 28-day completion deadline typically needs funds released within 2 to 3 weeks. Rates here tend to sit slightly higher, often 0.70% to 0.85% a month, because the lender prices in the compressed timeline and reduced due diligence window. The trade-off is usually worth it, since missing an auction completion deadline can mean losing the 10% deposit entirely. Clients looking into bridging loans in London and bridging loans in Norwich for auction purchases should factor in the same compressed timeline when comparing lenders.

What lenders look for

Lenders want a clear, credible exit and enough equity in the security to cover their position if things go wrong. Loan-to-value on residential bridging typically sits between 65% and 75% of open market value, while commercial and development-led deals are usually 55% to 65%, sometimes assessed against gross development value rather than current value.

Timescales from enquiry to funds released usually run 7 to 21 working days for straightforward cases, and 3 to 6 weeks where there's a complex title, planning condition, or multiple securities involved. Acceptable security includes residential and commercial property, land with or without planning, and in some cases a mix of assets across a portfolio.

Evidence of exit is where most applications either sail through or stall. Lenders want to see a sale agreed, a mortgage agreement in principle, a refinance offer, or a clear development timeline with realistic sales projections. The most common reason we see applications declined isn't affordability, it's a weak or vague exit strategy, something like "I'll probably sell it eventually" rather than a documented plan with dates and figures attached.

Credit history matters less in bridging than in mainstream mortgage lending, but it isn't ignored. Most bridging loan lenders will still run a credit check and want to understand any adverse history, particularly around mortgage arrears or CCJs registered in the last two years. A poor credit history won't necessarily kill an application, but it can push the rate up or reduce the maximum LTV a lender is willing to offer. For a closer look at how different lenders assess these cases, see our review of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK.

Lenders also look closely at the quality and location of the security itself. A standard three-bed semi in a strong commuter town will typically get a faster, more competitive response than a flat above a commercial unit or a property in a rural area with limited comparable sales. Non-standard construction, short leases under 70 years, or properties above certain types of retail units can all lead to reduced LTVs or a smaller pool of lenders willing to consider the deal at all.

Finally, remember that a bridging finance calculator, however detailed, can never fully replace a conversation with a broker who knows which lenders are actively pricing keenly for your specific scenario that month. Rates and appetite shift regularly, and the cheapest headline rate on a comparison table isn't always available once you factor in your actual LTV, security type and required completion date. Running the numbers yourself is a sensible first step, but treat it as the opening move rather than the final answer.

Costs to budget for beyond the headline rate

Beyond the interest rate itself, keep a running checklist of every fee mentioned above so nothing catches you out at completion: arrangement fee, valuation fee, legal costs on both sides, any exit fee, and a buffer for a possible extension. Lenders offering bridging loans will usually confirm these figures in a decision in principle before you commit to a full application, so ask for this in writing early rather than relying on the calculator alone. Building this checklist into your own planning, alongside a realistic view of your exit timeline, is the single best way to avoid the true cost of short-term property finance running ahead of what you budgeted.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does a bridging finance calculator actually show you?
It shows an estimated monthly interest figure based on the loan amount, term and rate you enter. It typically won't include arrangement fees, valuation costs, legal fees or exit fees, so the real cost of borrowing is usually higher than the headline figure.

How much do arrangement fees usually add to a bridging loan?
Most lenders charge between 1.5% and 2% of the loan amount as an arrangement fee. This is usually added to the loan itself rather than paid upfront in cash, which means it also increases the amount interest is charged on.

What's the difference between rolled-up, retained and serviced interest?
Rolled-up interest is added to the loan and repaid at the end. Retained interest is deducted from the advance upfront, reducing the cash you receive on day one. Serviced interest is paid monthly from income, which keeps total borrowing lower but requires proof of affordability.

How quickly can bridging finance be arranged?
Straightforward cases typically complete in 7 to 21 working days. More complex cases involving multiple securities, planning conditions or a complicated title can take 3 to 6 weeks.

What happens if I repay a bridging loan early?
It depends on the lender. Some charge a minimum term of one to three months' interest even if you redeem early, while others allow repayment at any point without penalty. It's worth checking this before you commit, as it can make a significant difference to the total cost.

What do lenders look for when assessing a bridging application?
Lenders focus heavily on a clear, credible exit strategy, whether that's a sale agreed, a refinance offer, or a mortgage agreement in principle. They also assess the loan-to-value, the quality and location of the security, and any adverse credit history.

Can I get a bridging loan if I have poor credit?
Often yes, since bridging lenders weigh credit history less heavily than mainstream mortgage lenders. However, adverse credit such as arrears or CCJs in the last two years can push the rate up or reduce the maximum LTV on offer.

For a full breakdown of costs, LTVs and exit strategies tailored to your situation, visit our bridging finance funding solutions page, explore our full range of business funding solutions, or get a bridging finance calculator quote from our team today.
