content:
Bridging loans in the UK property market in 2026 are being used more heavily than ever to solve timing problems: buying before selling, completing on auction lots within 28 days, or funding a refurbishment before a property qualifies for a mortgage. Bridging loans uk property market 2026 finance fills the gap between needing to act now and a longer-term funding solution being ready, and demand has grown as mortgage chains stretch and lenders tighten standard criteria.

We've arranged many of these deals over the past twelve months, and the pattern is consistent. Buyers and developers who understand exactly what a bridging loan is for, and what it costs, complete the process quickly. Those who treat it as a cheap alternative to a mortgage get a shock at the interest rate or, worse, face last-minute decline because their exit strategy isn't credible. This article sets out where bridging loans genuinely fit in the 2026 market and where they don't.

What this means in practice

In practice, a bridging loan is a short-term secured loan, usually against property, arranged in weeks rather than months and priced monthly rather than annually. It exists to bridge a gap that a mortgage or long-term facility cannot fill quickly enough.

For residential buyers, that gap is often a broken chain: you've exchanged on your purchase but your own sale has fallen through, or you've won at auction and have 28 days to complete. For landlords, it might be buying an unmortgageable property, refurbishing it, then refinancing onto a standard buy-to-let mortgage once it's habitable and let. For developers, it's typically funding the acquisition and works on a conversion or small development, then exiting via sale of the units or a term refinance once practical completion is reached.

What changes in 2026 is the backdrop. Base rate has settled lower than its 2023 peak but lender margins on short-term property finance haven't fallen as much as borrowers hoped, because underwriting costs and fraud checks have increased. Meanwhile more high street lenders have pulled back from unusual security types, pushing more legitimate deals toward specialist bridging lenders. That's widened the market for brokers like Boxx Commercial Finance, but it also means shopping around on rate matters more than ever.

How it works

A bridging loan works by securing the debt against property, valuing that property (or the end value after works, known as GDV for developers), and setting a maximum loan against that value with monthly interest, usually rolled up rather than paid monthly out of your pocket.

Most bridging loans in the UK today run for three to eighteen months, though 2026 has seen more twelve-month products appear as lenders build in extra buffer for slower sales chains. Interest typically runs from around 0.55% to 1.1% per month depending on the loan-to-value, the security type and how clean the exit is. That's before arrangement fees, which usually sit between 1.5% and 2% of the loan, plus valuation and legal costs.

Crucially, the loan is priced on the exit. A lender wants to know exactly how you'll repay: sale of the security property, sale of another asset, or refinance onto a term mortgage. The stronger and more evidenced that exit, the better the rate you'll be offered. We always tell clients this upfront because it changes how you should present the deal from day one.

If you're ready to explore your options, you can get a bridging loan quote with a broker before you commit to a lender.

Typical scenarios

Two scenarios come up again and again in 2026, one residential and one developer-led.

A first-time landlord in Reading found a three-bed terrace at auction, priced to sell because of an outdated kitchen and bathroom and no current mortgage certificate of compliance. She needed £145,000 against a £230,000 purchase price (63% LTV) over a 9-month term, with the exit being a refinance onto a standard buy-to-let mortgage once the works were done and the property re-let. Funds were released in 11 working days, well inside the 28-day auction deadline. Landlords buying through bridging loans in Reading follow this pattern more often than anywhere else we see, largely because of the volume of auction stock in that region.

A small developer in Birmingham was converting a former office building into six flats. They needed £680,000 against a GDV of £1.1 million (62% LTV against GDV, released in stages as works progressed), over an 18-month term, exiting via sale of the completed units. Because the developer had a strong track record of two previous conversions, the lender released the first tranche in 15 working days rather than the more typical three to four weeks for a first-time developer. Developers arranging bridging loans in Birmingham and other regional cities are increasingly using staged drawdowns like this to control interest costs across the build.

What lenders look for

Lenders want a clean, evidenced exit above almost everything else. In our experience, the single biggest reason applications get declined is a vague or unrealistic exit strategy rather than the security or the LTV.

Loan-to-value ranges in 2026 typically run up to 70-75% on residential security and 60-65% on commercial or development security, though this drops for unusual or unmortgageable assets. Timescales from full application to funds released usually run 10 to 20 working days for a straightforward residential bridge, and three to six weeks for a development deal needing staged monitoring. Lenders will accept most property types as security, including semi-commercial, land with planning, and HMOs, but they'll always want an independent valuation and, for developments, a monitoring surveyor's sign-off at each stage.

On the exit, lenders expect real evidence, not just intention. For a sale exit, that means comparable evidence of value and, ideally, an estate agent's marketing appraisal. For a refinance exit, they want an agreement in principle from the receiving lender before completion, not after. Lenders rarely state this explicitly, but a bridging application with a refinance exit and no AIP attached is treated with real suspicion, as this is the number one reason bridges overrun their term. The other common decline reason is undisclosed adverse credit turning up in underwriting that wasn't flagged at application stage. Be upfront about this from the start; it rarely kills a deal on its own, but hiding it always causes delay or refusal.

Common mistakes

The most common mistake we see is borrowers underestimating total cost by only looking at the monthly rate and ignoring arrangement fees, exit fees, valuation costs and legal fees on both sides.

A close second is applying without a firm plan B on the exit. If your exit is refinance and the receiving lender pulls out, or your exit is sale and the market softens, you need a fallback. A good broker will ask you this before the lender does. We've seen deals stall for weeks simply because nobody had thought about what happens if the sale takes longer than expected.

Timing is another frequent trap. Borrowers often start the bridging process too close to their deadline, particularly with auction purchases, leaving no room for a valuation delay or a title issue found by the solicitor. Starting the conversation with a broker as soon as you have a target property, even before you've had an offer accepted, gives you far more room to negotiate rate and terms rather than accepting whatever's available under time pressure.

Alternatives or comparisons

Bridging loans are the wrong choice if you have more than a few months to arrange finance and could instead qualify for a standard mortgage or a development finance facility at a lower rate. If your exit is uncertain or speculative, don't take a bridge; the interest will compound against you every month it overruns.

For a straightforward house purchase with no chain break and no urgency, a standard residential mortgage will always be cheaper. For larger ground-up developments running beyond 18 months, dedicated development finance with drawdowns tied to build stages usually works out more cost-effective than a short-term property finance facility, because it's priced for the full build cycle rather than a short-term gap. And if you simply need working capital for your business rather than solving a property timing issue, an unsecured business loan or asset finance is usually a better fit than putting property up as security. Our plain-English guide to how bridging finance works is worth reading if you're still deciding whether it's the right tool at all.

How to get the best outcome

The best outcome comes from having your exit evidenced before you apply, not after. Get your AIP in hand, your valuation appraisal ready, and your solicitor instructed early.

Rate shopping matters too. The spread between lenders on a comparable deal can be 0.2% to 0.3% per month, which adds up fast over a nine or twelve month term. Checking current UK bridging loan rates before you commit, and comparing more than one lender's terms rather than accepting the first offer, routinely saves clients several thousand pounds. It's also worth reviewing how the main UK bridging lenders compare on speed and flexibility, not just headline rate, since the cheapest lender on paper isn't always the fastest to complete.

If you want to talk through a live purchase or refinance need, take the time to compare bridging loan rates properly before committing to a lender, because the terms on offer vary significantly. You can also arrange a bridging loan today with our team.

Summary

Bridging loans remain one of the most useful tools in the UK property market for 2026, provided they're used for what they're designed for: solving a genuine, short-term timing gap with a credible, evidenced exit. Used well, they unlock deals that would otherwise be lost. Used carelessly, they're an expensive way to buy time you didn't plan for properly.

Whether you're a landlord bidding at auction, a homeowner covering a broken chain, or a developer funding a conversion, working through the numbers with a broker before you commit will save you money and stress. Boxx Commercial Finance arranges these deals across the country, including bridging loans in London and bridging loans in Norwich, and we're happy to talk through whether a bridge is genuinely the right tool for your situation or whether one of the wider UK commercial funding solutions would serve you better.

If you're weighing up a purchase, refurbishment or chain-break situation, arrange a bridging loan conversation with a broker who can look at your exact numbers before you commit to anything. To get started, get a bridging loan quote or find a bridging loan broker today.

Frequently Asked Questions

How quickly can a bridging loan complete in 2026?
Most straightforward residential bridging loans complete in 10 to 20 working days once all documents are submitted. Development or commercial deals needing staged monitoring typically take three to six weeks. Auction purchases with tight 28-day deadlines are achievable but leave little room for delays, so early instruction matters.
What is the maximum loan-to-value on a bridging loan?
Residential security typically supports up to 70-75% LTV, while commercial or development security is usually capped around 60-65%. Unusual or unmortgageable properties often see lower maximum LTVs due to the added valuation risk lenders are taking on.
Are bridging loan interest rates rising or falling in 2026?
Rates have stabilised compared to the 2023 peak but haven't fallen as fast as base rate, typically sitting between 0.55% and 1.1% per month. Lender margins remain firm because underwriting and fraud-check costs have increased, so shopping around still makes a real difference to total cost.
Can I get a bridging loan with bad credit?
Yes, many specialist lenders will consider adverse credit provided it's disclosed upfront and the security and exit are strong. Undisclosed adverse credit discovered during underwriting is one of the most common reasons applications stall or get declined, so honesty at application stage is essential.
What happens if I can't repay my bridging loan on time?
Most lenders allow a short extension if you can evidence the exit is progressing, though this usually comes with an extension fee and continued interest. If there's no credible progress, the lender can move toward repossession, which is why having a clear fallback exit before you apply matters so much.
Is a bridging loan cheaper than a development finance facility?
For short gaps of a few months, bridging is usually cheaper and faster to arrange than development finance. For larger builds running beyond 18 months with staged drawdowns tied to construction milestones, dedicated development finance is normally more cost-effective over the full build cycle.

title: Bridging Finance for Change of Use Properties
excerpt: A bridging loan for change of use lets you buy or refinance a property before planning consent is granted, exiting once the new use class is confirmed and the asset revalues.
metaTitle: Bridging Finance for Change of Use Properties
metaDescription: How a bridging loan for change of use works, what lenders want to see, real deal figures, and when this type of short-term property finance is the wrong choice.
keywords: change of use bridging loan, bridging loan planning permission, developer finance change of use, short-term property finance, bridging loan for property conversion, commercial to residential bridging loan, planning gain bridging finance
author: Mark Higgins
content:
A bridging loan for change of use is short-term property finance used to purchase or refinance a building before planning permission for its new use class has been granted. Lenders assess the property on its current use and value, then price in the planning risk, allowing developers and investors to move quickly on a site while the local authority decision is still pending. The exit is usually a refinance or sale once consent is confirmed.

We arrange this type of lending regularly at Boxx Commercial Finance, and it's one of the more misunderstood corners of the bridging market. Borrowers often assume lenders will simply refuse to touch a property without planning permission in place. That's not true. What they will do is price the uncertainty into the loan-to-value and, occasionally, the rate. Understanding how that pricing works is the difference between a smooth application and a wasted week chasing lenders who were never going to say yes. If you'd like to talk through a specific site, you can get a bridging loan quote before you commit to anything.

We see this scenario play out several times a month. A client spots a former bank branch on a high street, or a tired care home, or a redundant agricultural barn, and immediately sees the residential or commercial potential. The trouble is that potential exists only on paper until the council agrees. Short-term property finance is what lets you own the asset while that agreement is being sought. For a broader introduction to how this lending works, our guide on what bridging finance actually is is a useful starting point.

Not every case involves a full planning application from scratch. Plenty of our enquiries relate to properties with permitted development rights already in place, where the works themselves are relatively straightforward, but the borrower still needs to complete a purchase before the prior approval process has run its course. Lenders treat these slightly differently to a full discretionary planning application, usually with greater comfort around timescale and outcome.

What this means in practice

In practice, it means you can secure a property, start the planning process, or complete works ahead of a formal use class change, without waiting for the council to make its decision before you can access funding.

This matters because good sites don't wait around. A commercial unit with obvious residential conversion potential, or a pub with permitted development rights into flats, often sells fast, sometimes at auction, sometimes off-market to whoever can complete first. If your funding is contingent on planning being granted, you'll lose the property to someone using bridging loans instead.

Take a typical example we've dealt with. A client wanted to buy a vacant office building in the Midlands for £450,000, with a clear plan to convert it into eight flats under permitted development rights. Planning wasn't yet submitted. A bridging lender agreed to lend 65% against the current office valuation, around £292,500, allowing the purchase to complete within three weeks. Had the client waited for planning consent before arranging finance, the vendor would almost certainly have sold to a cash buyer instead.

To put the wider cost into context, that £292,500 loan at a monthly rate of 0.85% would cost roughly £2,486 per month in interest, most of which is typically rolled up rather than paid monthly, so the borrower isn't drawing that from cashflow each month. Over a nine month term while planning was progressed and the flats prepared for sale or refinance, the rolled interest would total around £22,370, plus arrangement fees. Clients are often surprised how manageable that figure looks once it's set against the profit on eight completed flats.

The lender's underwriting reflects the current, unconsented use. A disused office block is valued and lent against as an office block, not as the block of flats it might become. The uplift in value that comes with planning consent is your equity gain, not something most bridging lenders will lend against upfront.

Loan-to-value, rates and fees

A handful of specialist lenders will consider gross development value or a probable-use valuation once a planning application has actually been submitted, particularly if the local planning history for that street or area shows a strong pattern of approvals. This is rarely offered on day one. It tends to come into play once you can show the council has acknowledged the application and there are no obvious objections on file.

Loan-to-value on these deals typically sits between 55% and 70% of the current use value, depending on the lender, the location, and how straightforward the planning story is. A straightforward office-to-residential conversion under permitted development rights is viewed very differently to a full change of use application on a listed building in a conservation area. The latter carries far more planning risk, and lenders will reflect that in a lower LTV or a higher rate. For a wider view of current pricing, see our breakdown of current bridging loan rates across the market.

Rates on change of use bridging in the current market tend to range from around 0.65% to 1.1% per month, depending on the loan size, the borrower's experience, and the perceived planning risk. A borrower with a strong track record of similar conversions, backed by a solicitor and planning consultant who know the local authority well, will usually secure sharper pricing than a first-time developer with no comparable projects behind them.

Arrangement fees typically sit between 1.5% and 2% of the gross loan, with some lenders also charging an exit fee, though many of the more competitive lenders in this space have moved away from exit fees to stay attractive. It's worth checking the total cost of the facility rather than focusing purely on the headline monthly rate, since some lenders load fees at the front end while others spread cost differently across the term.

On a £300,000 loan, a 2% arrangement fee works out at £6,000, deducted from the gross advance rather than paid upfront in most cases. Add valuation fees of anywhere between £500 and £1,500 depending on the property type and complexity, plus legal costs which often run to £1,500 to £2,500 for the borrower's own solicitor, and it becomes clear why the all-in cost of a bridge needs setting out clearly before a client commits. We always send clients a full breakdown before they instruct anyone, so there are no surprises at completion.

Term length and timing

Term length usually runs from six to eighteen months, giving enough runway to submit a planning application, go through committee if needed, and then arrange a refinance or sale once consent is granted. Six months is often too tight if there's any chance of a planning appeal or a resubmission, so we generally encourage clients to build in some contingency rather than cutting it fine.

We've seen cases where a straightforward application was expected to take eight weeks, then dragged on for five months because of a single objection from a neighbour or a request for further ecological surveys. Building a realistic buffer into the loan term avoids the scramble of arranging an extension under pressure, which rarely gets you the best terms from a lender.

Speed of completion is one of the main reasons borrowers choose this route in the first place. Where a standard mortgage application might take eight to twelve weeks, a bridging loan for change of use can often complete in two to four weeks, sometimes faster if the valuation and legal work move quickly. That speed is usually the whole point, since it's what allows you to beat other buyers to a site with obvious conversion potential.

In practical terms, that timeline depends heavily on how quickly the borrower can provide certain documents. Proof of funds for any deposit, a clear schedule of works or planning intentions, ID and source of funds paperwork, and details of any other properties owned all need to be ready early. Clients who gather this before the application even starts routinely shave a week or more off the process compared with those chasing paperwork mid-application.

Exit strategy and lender expectations

We always advise clients to get their planning consultant involved before they even approach a lender. A short pre-application enquiry with the local authority, even an informal one, can give a lender far more comfort than a bare application with no local authority engagement at all. It also helps establish realistic timescales, since some councils are notoriously slower than others in reaching a decision.

Exit strategy is scrutinised closely by lenders on these deals, arguably more closely than on a standard bridging case. Because the loan is priced against current use rather than the uplifted value, lenders want to see a credible route out once planning is granted. That's usually either a term mortgage refinance based on the new use, or a sale to an investor or owner-occupier who wants the converted asset.

Some lenders will ask for evidence of an agreement in principle from a term lender before they'll release funds, particularly on larger facilities. Others are comfortable relying on the strength of the borrower's track record and the general market appetite for the finished product, whether that's flats, an HMO, or commercial units. It varies quite a bit between lenders, which is where a broker's knowledge of individual lender appetite becomes genuinely useful. Choosing the right lender matters here, and our comparison of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK is worth reading before you approach anyone directly.

Rural sites and permitted development

We also see a fair amount of change of use bridging on rural and semi-rural sites, particularly barn conversions and redundant agricultural buildings being converted to residential use under Class Q permitted development rights. These cases carry their own quirks, since Class Q has specific criteria around the building's structural condition and size that can affect both the planning outcome and the lender's comfort with the deal.

Structural surveys often play a bigger part in these rural cases than borrowers expect. A barn that looks solid enough to convert on the surface can be rejected under Class Q if it needs substantial rebuilding rather than conversion, and lenders will usually want a structural engineer's report early on to confirm the building genuinely qualifies. Getting this wrong can unravel a deal weeks into the process, so it's far better checked before finance is even applied for.

Because every case is different, and because lender appetite for planning risk shifts fairly often depending on market conditions, it's worth speaking to a broker who places this type of lending regularly rather than approaching lenders directly one by one. At Boxx Commercial Finance, we work with a panel of lenders who each treat planning risk differently, and matching the right lender to the right site is usually what makes the difference between a deal that completes smoothly and one that stalls. We arrange this lending for clients seeking bridging loans in London, bridging loans in Birmingham, bridging loans in Norwich, and bridging loans in Reading, among many other locations across the UK.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I get a bridging loan without planning permission in place?
Yes. Lenders will assess the property on its current use and value, then price the planning risk into the loan-to-value and, in some cases, the rate. A full consent isn't required to secure funding.

What loan-to-value can I expect on a change of use bridging loan?
Typically between 55% and 70% of the current use value, depending on the lender, the location, and how straightforward the planning story is.

How much does a bridging loan for change of use cost?
Rates generally range from around 0.65% to 1.1% per month, with arrangement fees of 1.5% to 2% of the gross loan, plus valuation and legal costs on top.

How long does it take to complete a bridging loan for change of use?
Often two to four weeks, compared with eight to twelve weeks for a standard mortgage, provided valuation and legal work move quickly.

What exit strategy do lenders expect on these deals?
Usually a term mortgage refinance based on the new use, or a sale to an investor or owner-occupier once planning consent is granted.

Do lenders treat permitted development rights differently to full planning applications?
Yes. Cases involving permitted development rights are generally viewed with more comfort around timescale and outcome than a full discretionary planning application.

How long is the typical loan term?
Usually between six and eighteen months, giving enough time to submit a planning application, deal with any objections, and arrange a refinance or sale once consent is granted.

If you're weighing up a site with planning potential, it's worth speaking to a specialist early. You can explore our wider funding solutions for property investors or get a bridging loan quote with our team.

title: Bridging Loans Without a Personal Guarantee
excerpt: Personal guarantees are standard on most bridging loans, but limited-guarantee and no-PG structures do exist for the right deal. Here is how they actually work and who qualifies.
metaTitle: Bridging Loans Without a Personal Guarantee
metaDescription: Bridging Loans Without a Personal Guarantee. Expert advice from Boxx Commercial Finance, a whole-of-market UK bridging finance broker.
keywords: bridging loan no personal guarantee UK, limited personal guarantee bridging loan, bridging loans for limited companies, developer finance no personal guarantee, short-term property finance without PG, bridging loan security requirements, non-recourse bridging finance UK
author: Andrew Farrimond

mainEntity.name: Can I really get a bridging loan with no personal guarantee?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, but only on a minority of deals, typically where the loan-to value sits below 50-55%, the exit is contractually secure, and the borrowing entity has a strong track record. Most borrowers end up with a limited or capped guarantee rather than a true zero-PG structure.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a limited guarantee and no personal guarantee?

acceptedAnswer.text: A limited guarantee caps the director's personal exposure at a set percentage of the loan, often 15-25%, while a no personal guarantee deal removes personal recourse entirely. Limited guarantees are far more common and easier to negotiate than a full removal.

mainEntity.name: Do all bridging lenders offer no personal guarantee options?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Only a subset of specialist lenders will consider it, and usually only for low-LTV deals with strong exits. Approaching lenders who do not offer this structure wastes time, so it pays to check with a broker who knows the panel first.

mainEntity.name: Will a no personal guarantee bridging loan cost more?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often yes, either through a lower maximum LTV, a shorter term, or a slightly higher margin, because the lender is giving up a cheap form of security. The trade-off is usually worth it for directors keen to protect personal assets.

mainEntity.name: Does my company structure affect whether I can avoid a personal guarantee?

acceptedAnswer.text: Significantly. A clean special purpose vehicle with no cross-charges to other companies and a clear ownership structure is viewed far more favourably than a group with related-party loans or unclear beneficial ownership.

mainEntity.name: What LTV do I need for a lender to consider dropping the personal guarantee?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most lenders we deal with will only consider it below roughly 50-55% LTV. Above 65% LTV, a full personal guarantee is almost always required regardless of the borrower's track record or the strength of the exit.

mainEntity.name: Is a no personal guarantee bridging loan available for first-time investors?

acceptedAnswer.text: Realistically, no. Lenders want a demonstrable track record before removing personal recourse. First-time investors should expect a full personal guarantee and focus instead on negotiating the rate and fees.

content:
A bridging loan without a personal guarantee is possible but uncommon. Lenders will only agree to this when they hold strong security elsewhere and do not need a director's personal covenant. Most bridging loan options in the real market are actually limited guarantees rather than a true zero-PG deal, and understanding that distinction will save you significant time.

We receive enquiries about this most weeks, usually from a director who has been burned before or who simply does not want their personal assets tied to a company borrowing. The question is fair. Lenders price risk against certainty, and a personal guarantee is one of the cheapest ways for them to get that certainty. Remove it and something else has to give. If you want to understand the fundamentals first, our guide to what bridging finance actually involves is a useful starting point.

What this means in practice

In practice, a no personal guarantee bridging loan means the lender is relying entirely on the property asset and the deal structure to cover their exposure, with no recourse to the borrower's personal wealth if things go wrong.

For most SME directors and property investors, that sounds ideal. Nobody wants their house on the line for a business loan. But lenders are not charities. If they cannot call on a personal guarantee, they will usually want a lower loan-to-value, stronger asset quality, a shorter term, or a materially higher margin to compensate.

The deals that genuinely proceed without any PG share three features: low leverage (typically under 50% LTV), a very clean, liquid exit such as a pre-agreed sale, and a corporate borrower with a track record the lender trusts. Remove any one of those and the lender starts asking for a guarantee again.

It is also worth separating true no-PG deals from limited or capped guarantees, which are far more common. A limited guarantee might cap personal exposure at 20% of the loan rather than 100%, which achieves most of what borrowers actually want without the lender losing all their leverage. Our breakdown of current bridging loan rates across the UK shows how pricing shifts once a guarantee is reduced or removed.

How it works

The mechanics start with how the lender views the security. If the property alone, once revalued conservatively, comfortably covers the loan and the lender's costs of enforcement, a personal guarantee becomes less critical to their risk model.

Lenders typically look at loan-to-value first. Deals under 50% LTV open the door to guarantee-free or limited-guarantee structures because there is enough equity cushion to absorb a forced sale at a discount. Above 65% LTV, most lenders insist on a full personal guarantee regardless of who the borrower is.

Next comes the exit. A bridging loan without a personal guarantee is much easier to arrange when the exit is refinance onto a term facility with an agreement in principle already in place, or a sale with an exchanged contract. Lenders dislike uncertainty, and removing the PG removes their fallback, so they need the exit risk minimised elsewhere.

Company structure matters too. Special purpose vehicles with a clean balance sheet, no cross-charging to other assets, and directors with a demonstrable track record in property or development attract far more favour. A first-time investor with a thin company and no trading history is highly unlikely to secure a no-PG deal at any LTV. This applies whether you are arranging bridging loans in London or looking at opportunities further afield.

Some lenders also look at debenture and fixed/floating charge structures across the company as an alternative to personal recourse. This gives them a claim on company assets without touching the director personally, which can be a workable middle ground.

Typical scenarios

A developer in Manchester needed £950,000 against a completed block of four flats valued at £2.1 million (45% LTV) over a 10-month term, exiting via pre-sold units with contracts already exchanged on three of the four. Because the LTV was low and the exit was contractually secured, the lender agreed a limited personal guarantee capped at 15% of the loan, and funds were released in 16 working days.

Contrast that with a residential landlord in Norwich who needed £180,000 against a £260,000 buy-to-let (69% LTV) to complete an auction purchase within 28 days. At that leverage, with a straightforward refinance exit and no pre-agreed sale, the lender required a full personal guarantee. No realistic route existed to a limited or no-PG structure given the LTV, and pushing for one would have cost weeks the client did not have. Clients arranging bridging loans in Norwich often face this same LTV constraint on auction purchases.

We arrange bridging loans for both types of client, but the developer scenario above is far more representative of where a genuine reduction in personal guarantee actually happens. We also regularly place bridging loans in Birmingham and bridging loans in Reading under similar limited-guarantee terms.

What lenders look for

Lenders assessing a limited or no personal guarantee bridging loan look for low leverage, a clean exit strategy, and a borrower entity strong enough to stand on its own. All three of these must be right, not just one or two.

Typical LTV ranges for guarantee-free consideration sit at 40-55%. Above that, expect a full PG requirement from nearly every mainstream bridging lender we deal with. Timescales from enquiry to funds tend to run 10-20 working days once valuation and legals are instructed, though complex corporate structures can push this to four or five weeks.

Acceptable security is almost always a first legal charge over UK property, sometimes supported by a debenture over company assets or a second charge over an additional property if one is available. Lenders require independent valuation evidence, a solicitor's report on title, and clear proof of the exit route, whether that is a signed sale contract, an agreement in principle for refinance, or evidence of rental income supporting a term mortgage.

The most common reason we see these applications declined is over-optimistic LTV expectations. Directors approach us wanting 70% LTV with no personal guarantee, and that combination simply does not exist in this market. The second most common reason is a weak or unproven exit, particularly speculative sales with no marketing evidence or comparable evidence behind the valuation. If you want a clearer sense of who actually offers these structures, our review of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK covers this in more depth. In the meantime, you can get a bridging loan quote to see where your deal might sit.

Common mistakes

The biggest mistake is assuming that removing a personal guarantee is free. It never is. Borrowers who go into negotiations expecting no cost trade-off usually end up disappointed or delayed.

Another frequent error is applying to multiple lenders simultaneously without knowing which ones even offer limited guarantee structures. Not every lender in this space will consider it regardless of the deal quality, so approaching the wrong panel wastes time and can leave unnecessary credit search footprints.

Borrowers also commonly underestimate how much a clean corporate structure matters. A messy group structure with cross-guarantees to other companies, undisclosed related-party loans, or unclear beneficial ownership will kill a limited-guarantee request even on a strong asset, because the lender cannot get comfortable with what else they might be exposed to.

Lenders rarely state this outright, but a director who pushes too hard on removing personal liability early in a negotiation sometimes gets viewed with more suspicion, not less. It can read as a lack of confidence in their own exit. Raising it as one factor among several, rather than a dealbreaker from day one, tends to get a better hearing.

Alternatives or comparisons

If your deal sits above 60% LTV, has a speculative exit, or comes from a newly formed company with no track record, a no personal guarantee bridging loan is the wrong ambition. Pursuing one will cost you time and credibility with lenders for no real benefit.

In that situation, the better route is usually to accept a full personal guarantee but negotiate hard on rate, arrangement fee, and exit fee instead, or to bring in a second property as additional security to improve the LTV picture and open up more lender options generally. A joint venture partner with stronger covenant strength can also sometimes substitute for personal guarantee reduction.

For borrowers who fundamentally do not want personal exposure of any kind and cannot meet the low-LTV, clean-exit criteria above, mezzanine or equity finance may suit better than bridging, even though it costs more in the long run through profit share. It is a genuinely different trade-off and worth exploring with a broker who arranges both.

If you want to properly weigh up whether to push for a limited guarantee or accept standard terms, it is worth talking it through before you approach lenders. You can get a bridging loan quote and get a realistic view of what your specific deal will support before you commit to an application.

How to get the best outcome

The best outcome comes from matching your expectations to your deal's actual risk profile before you approach any lender, rather than negotiating guarantee terms after the fact.

Get an independent valuation opinion early, even an informal one, so you know roughly what LTV band you are in. If you are close to the 50-55% threshold, small adjustments like paying down a small amount or adding modest additional security can tip a deal from full-PG to limited-PG. Speak to a broker who can review your structure holistically and explore our full range of business funding solutions alongside short-term property finance, or get a bridging loan quote to see exactly where your deal stands.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it actually possible to get a bridging loan with no personal guarantee?
Yes, but only in a minority of cases. It typically requires low leverage, usually under 50% LTV, a clean and certain exit strategy, and a corporate borrower with a strong track record. Most deals that reduce personal exposure end up as limited guarantees rather than a true zero-PG arrangement.

What is the difference between a no personal guarantee and a limited personal guarantee?
A no personal guarantee deal removes all recourse to the borrower's personal assets. A limited guarantee caps that exposure, often at 15-20% of the loan amount, which is far more common and easier for lenders to agree to.

What LTV do I need to avoid a personal guarantee?
Most lenders will only consider guarantee-free or limited-guarantee structures at 40-55% LTV. Above 65% LTV, a full personal guarantee is almost always required regardless of the borrower's profile.

How long does it take to arrange a bridging loan without a personal guarantee?
Once valuation and legal work are instructed, most deals complete in 10-20 working days. More complex corporate structures, such as those involving debentures or multiple charges, can extend this to four or five weeks.

Why would a lender ask for a personal guarantee even on a strong asset?
Personal guarantees give lenders cheap additional certainty. If leverage is high, the exit is uncertain, or the corporate borrower has no track record, a lender will usually want that extra layer of security regardless of how strong the property itself looks.

What happens if my company structure is complicated?
Messy group structures with cross-guarantees, undisclosed related-party loans, or unclear beneficial ownership will usually stop a limited-guarantee request, even if the underlying asset is strong, because the lender cannot get comfortable with the wider risk.

Are there alternatives if I cannot get a no personal guarantee deal?
Yes. Options include negotiating harder on rate and fees while accepting a full guarantee, adding a second property as security, bringing in a joint venture partner, or considering mezzanine or equity finance if personal exposure is a dealbreaker.

title: What to Do When Your Mortgage Is Rejected: Bridging Loan Options in the UK

metaDescription: Mortgage declined after exchange or offer? Learn how a bridging loan when mortgage rejected UK works, what lenders need, and how fast funds can complete.

content:
A bridging loan when mortgage rejected uk is a short-term loan secured against property that replaces a declined mortgage so a purchase or refinance can still complete. Lenders assess the asset and the exit route rather than a lengthy affordability history, which is why funds can often be arranged in days rather than the weeks a mortgage application takes.

We see this scenario constantly. A buyer exchanges contracts, the mortgage offer is withdrawn at the eleventh hour because of a change in employment status, a down-valuation, or a lender pulling out of a niche property type, and suddenly there is a real risk of losing the deposit and the property. A bridging loan steps in to rescue the situation, buying time to either fix the mortgage application or arrange a longer-term refinance once the immediate pressure is off.

What makes this type of borrowing different from a standard mortgage decline appeal is speed of decision making. A mortgage underwriter working through a large lender's queue might take two or three weeks just to look at a case again, and that is assuming there is anything left to reconsider. A bridging lender, by contrast, is looking at the property, the loan-to-value, and whether there is a credible way to repay the loan within the term. That narrower focus is exactly why it works as a rescue tool when time has run out. If you want a fuller grounding in how this type of lending works before going further, our guide to what bridging finance actually is covers the basics well.

You should be honest about the cost trade-off too. Short-term property finance is more expensive per month than a mortgage, and nobody should pretend otherwise. But when the alternative is losing a deposit worth tens of thousands of pounds, or being sued for breach of contract on an exchanged purchase, a few months of bridging loan interest is usually the cheaper outcome by a wide margin. If you're weighing up whether this route makes sense for your situation, you can get a bridging loan quote before committing to anything.

What this means in practice

In practice it means treating the bridging loan as a temporary fix, not a permanent solution. You borrow against the property itself, complete the purchase or avoid losing it, and then refinance onto a standard mortgage or sell once your circumstances allow.

The most common trigger we see is a down-valuation. The buyer's mortgage offer was based on an agreed purchase price, the surveyor values it lower, and the lender reduces the loan accordingly, leaving a shortfall the buyer cannot cover from savings. Self-employed applicants whose most recent accounts show a dip in profit, contractors between contracts, and those with adverse credit picked up late in underwriting are the next most frequent group.

Another group we deal with regularly is buyers who have had an offer pulled because of last-minute changes to a lender's criteria rather than anything the borrower did wrong. A lender might suddenly stop accepting properties above a certain number of storeys, or above a shop, or with a flat roof extension, purely as an internal risk decision. None of that reflects on the borrower's ability to repay, but it still leaves them without a mortgage days before completion.

For property developers the picture looks slightly different. A development exit mortgage can be declined because the property is still unmortgageable in its current state, perhaps missing a kitchen or bathroom, or because the lender's criteria exclude properties above commercial units or with unusual construction. In these cases developer finance in the form of a short-term property loan covers the gap between practical completion and the point at which the unit meets standard mortgage criteria.

We also see this with auction purchases. Someone wins a lot at auction believing they have a mortgage agreed in principle, only to find the lender will not touch the property once full details are known, often because of short lease length or non-standard construction. Auction contracts typically require completion within 28 days, which is nowhere near enough time to source a new mortgage from scratch, so a bridging loan becomes the only realistic option to avoid losing the deposit and being pursued for the shortfall if the lot is resold at a loss.

How it works

The mechanics are straightforward: a lender values the property, agrees a loan against it, and releases funds once legal work is complete, usually secured by a first or second charge.

Most bridging loans in this scenario run for three to twelve months, though some lenders will go to eighteen or even twenty-four months if the exit is credible. Interest is typically rolled up or retained rather than paid monthly. This matters here because the borrower has usually just had a mortgage refused partly on affordability grounds, so a lender assessing serviceable monthly interest defeats the purpose.

Rolled up interest means the interest accrues and is added to the loan balance, paid off in full when the loan is redeemed. Retained interest means the lender deducts an agreed number of months' interest from the loan advance up front, so you receive slightly less on day one but make no ongoing payments. Both approaches suit a borrower who has just proven they cannot easily service monthly costs on paper, even if their actual cash flow is fine.

Loan-to-value tends to sit between 65% and 75% on residential property, sometimes higher with additional security. Rates for this type of rescue lending currently run from around 0.55% to 1.1% per month depending on loan size, property type and how clean the exit is. On a £250,000 loan over six months at 0.75% per month, for example, total interest would be in the region of £11,250, against a deposit and purchase that could be worth many multiples of that if the deal falls through instead. If you want a realistic sense of current pricing before you approach a lender, our piece on current UK bridging loan rates is worth reading first, and the wider UK SME lending rates data gives useful context on how the broader cost of borrowing is moving.

Arrangement fees typically run from 1% to 2% of the loan, and there will usually be a valuation fee and legal costs on top, often in the region of £500 to £1,500 depending on the property and whether the lender's solicitor and the borrower's solicitor act separately or jointly. A broker who works regularly with bridging lenders can often get these packaged and quoted clearly up front, which matters when you are already under time pressure and need to know exactly what completion will cost. It's also worth reading up on which bridging lenders suit rescue cases, since not every lender is set up to move quickly on a declined mortgage situation.

Typical scenarios

Real examples make this easier to picture than theory does.

A first-time buyer in Reading exchanged on a £340,000 flat. Two weeks before completion her mortgage lender withdrew the offer after a valuer flagged cladding issues on the building, even though the flat itself was unaffected. She needed £238,000 (70% LTV) over six months. We arranged a bridging loans in Reading facility that completed in nine working days, giving her time to secure an EWS1-friendly mortgage lender once the building's fire safety paperwork was updated.

A developer in Norwich had converted a former office into six flats. His exit mortgage on the final two units fell through because the lender's panel would not touch ex-commercial conversions less than six months old. He needed £310,000 against a combined value of £460,000 (67% LTV) over nine months, exiting via sale once the six-month seasoning period had passed. Funds were released in eleven working days through a bridging loans in Norwich arrangement, and both units sold within the term.

A landlord in Birmingham was refused a buy-to-let remortgage after his portfolio lender tightened stress-test rates. He needed £165,000 against a £270,000 property (61% LTV) over twelve months, exiting on a refinance with a different lender once rental income was reassessed under standard criteria. That deal, arranged as one of several bridging loans in Birmingham cases we've handled this year, completed in fourteen working days.

A couple in Manchester had their mortgage declined four days before exchange after the underwriter queried a gap in employment history that turned out to be paternity leave, incorrectly recorded by HR. There was no time to get the payslip evidence sorted and resubmit through the mortgage lender before the exchange deadline. A bridging loan of £192,000 against a £280,000 purchase (69% LTV) completed in eight working days, and they refinanced onto a normal mortgage six weeks later once the paperwork was corrected. Buyers in bigger cities, such as those needing bridging loans in London, often face the tightest deadlines simply because purchase chains and completion dates tend to be more compressed.

What lenders look for

Bridging lenders in this situation focus almost entirely on the property's value and the strength of the exit, not on why the mortgage was declined.

Expect loan-to-value offers between 65% and 75% on standard residential property, dropping to 55-60% on unusual construction, ex-local authority flats above the fourth floor, or properties with short leases. Commercial and semi-commercial security is usually capped lower, often 60-65%. Timescales from enquiry to funds typically run seven to fourteen working days where title is clean and the solicitor is responsive, though we have completed genuine emergencies in 72 hours when exchange deadlines were days away.

Lenders want documented proof of the exit. That means a mortgage agreement in principle from a named lender, a signed sale memorandum if you're selling, or a schedule of works and re-valuation timeline if the exit depends on the property becoming mortgageable. A vague statement that you plan to sort the mortgage out later will not get a case through credit committee, however good the property is.

Practical steps that speed things up considerably include instructing a solicitor who has handled bridging completions before, having proof of identity and proof of funds ready in advance, and being upfront about why the original mortgage was declined rather than letting the lender find out during underwriting. Most experienced brokers will also want sight of the original mortgage decline letter or broker notes, since this often shapes which bridging lender is the best fit and helps avoid presenting the case to a lender who will raise the same objection.

Finally, think about the exit from day one rather than treating it as an afterthought. A bridging loan without a clear, evidenced way to repay it within the agreed term is not a solution, it is just a more expensive way of delaying the same problem. Speaking to a broker early, ideally the moment a mortgage offer looks shaky rather than after it has been formally withdrawn, gives far more room to arrange the right facility on sensible terms.

Costs and fees to expect

Beyond the headline interest rate, you should budget for the full package of costs so there are no surprises at completion. Arrangement fees, valuation fees and legal costs all sit alongside the interest charged, and a broker who is used to arranging short-term property finance can usually set these out clearly before you commit to a lender.

Frequently Asked Questions

How quickly can a bridging loan complete after a mortgage is rejected?
Most cases complete in seven to fourteen working days where the title is clean and the solicitor responds promptly, though genuine emergencies with days to spare before exchange have been completed in as little as 72 hours.

Will a bridging lender care why my mortgage was declined?
Not particularly. Bridging lenders focus on the property's value, the loan-to-value, and whether there is a credible, evidenced exit route, rather than on the reasons behind the original mortgage refusal.

What loan-to-value can I expect on a rescue bridging loan?
Typically 65% to 75% on standard residential property, dropping to 55-60% on unusual construction or short-lease flats, and often 60-65% on commercial or semi-commercial security.

Do I have to make monthly payments on a bridging loan?
Not usually. Interest is normally rolled up or retained, meaning it's added to the loan balance or deducted upfront, so there are no ongoing monthly payments to service.

What proof of exit does a lender need to see?
A mortgage agreement in principle from a named lender, a signed sale memorandum if you're selling, or a schedule of works and re-valuation timeline if the exit depends on the property becoming mortgageable.

How much does a bridging loan cost compared with losing a deposit?
Rates typically run from around 0.55% to 1.1% per month plus arrangement and legal fees, which is almost always far cheaper than losing a deposit worth tens of thousands of pounds or facing a breach of contract claim.

Can I use a bridging loan for an auction purchase with a tight deadline?
Yes, this is one of the most common uses, since auction contracts usually require completion within 28 days, which is rarely enough time to arrange a fresh mortgage from scratch.

If your mortgage has just fallen through and you need a fast, structured way forward, our funding specialists can talk you through the options on our funding solutions hub, or you can go straight ahead and get a bridging loan quote.

content:
The best company structure for a bridging loan depends on your exit strategy, tax position and how many properties you plan to hold. Most UK property investors use a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) limited company, most developers use a trading limited company, and most homeowners simply borrow in their personal name. Bridging loans can be arranged through any of these structures, but the wrong choice adds cost, delay or an unwelcome tax bill down the line.

We get asked this question almost every week, usually by someone who has already found a property and wants funds moving fast. The honest answer is that there isn't one universally correct structure. The correct structure depends on your circumstances, and getting it wrong before you apply can cost you weeks you don't have. If you want clarity on your own deal early on, you can get a bridging loan quote before you commit to a purchase.

What this means in practice

In practice, the structure you borrow through changes three things: how quickly a lender can complete, what rate and fees you're offered, and how the profit or rental income gets taxed once the deal is done. For an introduction to how these facilities work, our guide on what bridging finance actually involves is a useful starting point.

Borrowing personally is usually the fastest route because there's no company to search, no directors to verify beyond yourself, and no need to check the company's Articles of Association permit borrowing. If you're bridging to buy your own home, or breaking a chain on a residential purchase, personal name borrowing is almost always the sensible default.

An SPV limited company is the standard structure for buy-to-let investors and portfolio landlords. Lenders like SPVs because the company exists for one purpose, owning property, which makes underwriting cleaner and ring-fences liability. Most specialist bridging lenders now treat SPV lending as their standard offering rather than an exception.

A trading limited company, one that also runs an active business, lenders treat differently. Lenders will want to see the company's accounts and may ask for personal guarantees from directors regardless of the company's own assets. Developers running multiple sites through one trading company sometimes find lenders nervous about cross-contamination of liabilities between projects.

How it works

Once you know which entity is borrowing, the process is broadly the same: a valuation of the security property, legal due diligence, and a facility offer subject to conditions.

For personal borrowing, the lender assesses your income, credit history and the exit route, typically a sale or refinance onto a residential mortgage. Solicitors act for you and the lender, and completion on a straightforward case can happen in 7 to 14 working days.

For an SPV, the lender additionally checks the company's incorporation date, SIC codes (they'll want property-related codes registered), and requires personal guarantees from all directors owning more than around 20 to 25 percent of shares. Many lenders also want the SPV to have been dormant, meaning it has not traded anything else, which is why we always recommend setting up a clean SPV before you need funding rather than scrambling once you've found a deal.

For trading companies, expect a deeper look at the balance sheet, existing charges registered at Companies House, and often a debenture over company assets in addition to the property charge. This adds a few days to legal work but rarely derails a deal if the company's finances are in reasonable order.

Whichever structure you use, our team at Boxx Commercial Finance will usually flag at enquiry stage whether your chosen entity will slow things down, because catching it early saves a week later.

Typical scenarios

A first-time landlord in Reading wanted to buy a repossessed terrace at auction for £165,000, needing to complete within the standard 28-day auction window. She'd been advised to use an SPV for tax efficiency on future rental income. We arranged £115,000 (70% LTV) over a 6-month term, exiting via a buy-to-let remortgage once the property was tenanted. Because the SPV had been incorporated three weeks earlier with the correct SIC code and no trading history to complicate things, funds released in 11 working days, comfortably inside the auction deadline. If you're arranging bridging loans in Reading, this kind of turnaround is typical for a clean SPV case.

A developer client in Norwich was converting a former office building into six flats through his existing trading company, which also ran a small construction business. The lender insisted on a debenture and personal guarantees from both directors because of the trading history, adding roughly four days to legal work. We secured £480,000 against a £750,000 gross development value (64% LTV against GDV, with staged drawdowns), over 12 months, exiting on individual flat sales. Completion took 19 working days from initial enquiry, slower than the auction case above but still workable against his build programme. Developers arranging bridging loans in Norwich through an active trading company should budget for this kind of timescale.

What lenders look for

Lenders assess the entity, the security and the exit as three separate risk factors, and weakness in any one of them affects pricing even if the other two are strong.

Loan-to-value typically ranges from 65% to 75% for standard residential security, dropping to 50 to 60% for specialist or unusual assets like former agricultural buildings or properties with planning conditions still outstanding. Commercial security, including part-built developments, often sits at 60 to 65% of gross development value. For a breakdown of current pricing, see our overview of UK bridging loan rates and fees.

On timescales, a clean SPV case with a straightforward residential exit can complete in as little as 7 to 10 working days once instructions are given. Trading company cases with debentures, multiple charges, or cross-guarantees typically take 15 to 25 working days. Anything involving unregistered land or missing planning documentation can add another two to three weeks.

Lenders want firm evidence of the exit, not just an intention. For a sale exit, that means an estate agent's valuation and ideally a marketing plan. For a refinance exit, they want an Agreement in Principle from the onward lender before completion, not after. In our experience, the single most common reason bridging applications get declined at the eleventh hour is a weak or unevidenced exit, not the security itself.

A newly incorporated SPV with no trading history is often viewed more favourably than an established trading company with messy historic accounts, simply because there's nothing to unpick.

Common mistakes

The most frequent mistake is incorporating the wrong SPV, or the wrong SIC code, after already agreeing terms with a lender, which then delays legal work by days while corrections go through Companies House.

Another common error is borrowing personally when the intention is to hold the property long-term as a rental. This creates an unnecessary later step of transferring the property into a company, which usually triggers Stamp Duty Land Tax and potentially Capital Gains Tax on the transfer, on top of the costs already paid for the bridging loan itself.

We also see developers use their main trading company for a bridge when a fresh SPV would have kept the deal cleaner and quicker. If your trading company has other liabilities, charges or complex accounts, that history follows into the bridging application whether it's relevant to this specific deal or not.

Directors sometimes assume a personal guarantee won't be required because the company owns the asset outright. In reality, almost every specialist bridging lender in the UK requires personal guarantees from directors with meaningful shareholdings, regardless of company structure, so it's worth budgeting for that conversation with co-directors early rather than at the offer stage.

Alternatives or comparisons

A bridging loan through any structure is the wrong choice if your exit relies on hope rather than a credible plan, for example buying a property with no clear route to sale, refinance or completion of works within the agreed term. In that situation, a longer-term commercial mortgage or development finance facility with a realistic drawdown schedule is a better fit.

If you're an existing landlord simply looking to release equity from a property you already own outright, without a time-pressured purchase to fund, a standard buy-to-let remortgage is usually cheaper than a bridging loan and doesn't carry the same exit pressure.

For developers running several concurrent projects, a revolving development finance facility, rather than a series of individual bridging loans through one trading company, often proves more cost-effective once you're doing more than two or three projects a year.

How to get the best outcome

Set up your SPV, if you're going to use one, before you start viewing properties, not after you've had an offer accepted. This alone removes days from the legal timeline.

Get your Agreement in Principle for the exit route sorted in parallel with the bridging application, not after completion. Lenders want to see this evidenced, and it materially speeds up approval.

If you're unsure which structure fits your situation, it's worth talking it through before you commit to a purchase. You can compare bridging loan options for your structure with our team, who arrange these deals across personal, SPV and trading company borrowers every week and can tell you within a short conversation which route suits your specific deal. It's also worth taking a look at our review of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK before you approach anyone directly.

Rates and criteria also move with the wider lending market, so it's worth checking current UK SME lending rates before fixing on a particular lender, particularly if your deal has flexibility on timing.

Summary

There's no single best company structure for a bridging loan, but there is a right answer for your circumstances. Homeowners and chain-breakers should generally borrow personally, buy-to-let investors should use a clean SPV, and developers with active trading businesses need to plan for personal guarantees and slightly longer legal timescales. Get the structure right before you apply and the rest of the process moves considerably faster, whether you're arranging bridging loans in London, bridging loans in Birmingham, bridging loans in Norwich or bridging loans in Reading.

If you want to talk through the best structure for your own deal, our brokers arrange bridging loans for both first-time investors and established developers, and we can usually give you a clear answer on structure within a same-day call. Explore our wider UK commercial funding solutions if bridging turns out not to be the right fit once we've reviewed your circumstances.

For a straightforward next step, you can find a bridging loan broker who will look at your entity, your exit and your timescale together before recommending a lender, rather than pushing you towards whichever structure is quickest to process. content:
Bridging loans for unmortgageable property deals are one of the most common reasons buyers and developers come to us. A property becomes unmortgageable when it lacks a kitchen or bathroom, has no roof, suffers from structural issues, or has non-standard construction that high street lenders refuse outright. Our bridging loan service fills that gap by lending against the property's current condition and its future value once works are done, releasing funds in days rather than months.

Mainstream mortgage lenders assess risk on a tick-box basis. If a property does not meet their minimum habitability standard, the application is declined regardless of location or potential value. Bridging lenders take a different view entirely, and that difference is exactly why this corner of the market exists.

What this means in practice

You are not shut out of a purchase just because a bank says no. Bridging loans are secured lending products, typically arranged over 3 to 18 months, designed to bridge the gap between buying a property in poor or unusual condition and either selling it, refinancing it onto a standard mortgage, or completing works that make it lettable or saleable. For a fuller breakdown of how this product works, see our guide on what bridging finance actually involves.

For residential buyers this often means auction purchases where the property has been repossessed, fire-damaged, or simply neglected for years. For developers and landlords, it usually means a conversion, refurbishment, or a change of use project where the end value depends entirely on works being completed.

The lender's decision rests less on today's condition and more on the exit. If you can show a credible plan to get the property to a mortgageable standard, or a buyer lined up, most bridging lenders will engage where a bank would not even open the file.

How it works

A bridging loan for an unmortgageable property is underwritten against two figures: the current value in its existing condition, and the gross development value or GDV once works are complete. Lenders usually lend a percentage of the lower figure, or sometimes stage funding against the GDV if works are being funded too.

Most deals we arrange for this type of property sit between 65% and 75% loan-to-value against current value, with an additional facility released in stages for refurbishment costs if needed. Interest is usually rolled up or retained rather than paid monthly, which suits buyers who are not generating income from the property yet.

The valuer plays a significant role here. They will often provide two figures, the 'as is' value and the 'as converted' or 'as complete' value, and the lender's offer hinges on both. Getting a valuer who understands unmortgageable stock, rather than a generalist residential surveyor, genuinely speeds things up.

Once terms are agreed, legal work runs in parallel with valuation wherever possible. This is where working with a broker who knows which lenders move fast pays off, because timescales vary enormously across the market for this exact product. If you want to see how pricing compares across the market first, our overview of current bridging loan rates is a useful starting point, and if you would rather speak to us directly you can get a bridging loan quote.

Typical scenarios

We see two patterns repeatedly: one residential and one developer-led, both worth examining with real numbers.

A first-time landlord in Reading bought a two-bed flat at auction with no working kitchen or bathroom and damp throughout. She needed £145,000 against a purchase price of £190,000, an 76% LTV, over a 9-month term, with the exit being a remortgage onto a standard buy-to-let product once refurbishment was complete and the flat was tenanted. Funds released in 14 working days, tight for an auction completion but achievable because the solicitor and valuer were briefed early.

A developer in Norwich took on a former office building for residential conversion under permitted development rights. The building was structurally sound but had no residential use class and no habitable rooms, making it entirely unmortgageable in its existing form. The developer needed £620,000 against a £950,000 GDV, roughly 65% of GDV, over a 12-month term with staged drawdowns for the conversion works, exiting via sale of the completed units. That deal took 19 working days to first drawdown, which is realistic for a development-led facility of that size.

Both borrowers used short-term property finance because no mainstream lender would touch the property as it stood. Neither deal would have completed on a standard mortgage timeline, and both exits were planned before the loan was even agreed, which is exactly what lenders want to see.

What lenders look for

Lenders want a credible, evidenced exit above almost anything else, because that is what actually gets them repaid. A vague statement that you will 'sell it on' is not enough. They want a sales comparable, a mortgage agreement in principle for the refinance route, or a signed contract from a buyer.

Loan-to-value for unmortgageable property typically ranges from 60% to 75% of current value, occasionally higher against GDV for experienced developers with a strong track record. First-time landlords and developers should expect to sit at the more conservative end of that range, closer to 60-65%.

Timescales from enquiry to funds vary from as little as 7 working days for a simple, well-documented case, to 4-6 weeks where planning consent, building control sign-off, or complex title issues need resolving. Anyone buying at auction should assume the faster end is achievable only if paperwork is ready before the gavel falls.

Acceptable security includes residential property, mixed-use buildings, land with or without planning, and commercial premises being converted to residential. Lenders expect a schedule of works, a realistic costed budget, and often a contingency of 10-15% built in. Applications get declined most often because the applicant underestimated refurbishment costs, had no contingency, or could not evidence how the loan would be repaid within the term.

Lenders rarely state this outright, but a borrower's previous project history matters more than their credit score for these deals. A developer with two completed conversions behind them will get better terms than someone with a spotless credit file and zero experience, because the lender is really pricing execution risk, not just the security. It's worth reviewing our roundup of the best bridging loan lenders in the UK before approaching anyone directly.

Common mistakes

The single biggest mistake we see is buyers agreeing a purchase price before checking whether the property is even lendable against. Some conditions, such as severe structural movement or contamination, push certain lenders out entirely, and finding that out after exchange is a costly lesson.

Underestimating refurbishment costs is close behind. Borrowers who quote figures from a rough tradesperson estimate, rather than a proper schedule of works, frequently find the loan does not stretch far enough and end up needing a second charge or bridging top-up mid-project, which is expensive and avoidable.

Another recurring issue is assuming the exit will simply sort itself out. Lenders want to see the refinance or sale route mapped out from day one, not figured out in month eight of a nine-month term. We always push clients to have a fallback exit as well as a primary one.

Alternatives or comparisons

Short-term property finance is the wrong choice if the property could realistically be mortgaged with a specialist mainstream lender at a lower rate, or if your timeline genuinely allows for a standard purchase process. Some specialist mortgage lenders will lend on properties with minor cosmetic issues, and using one of those routes is cheaper if you qualify.

If the works needed are extensive and will take well over 18 months, a bridging loan is also the wrong tool, because rolled-up interest compounds and the cost escalates. In that case a full development finance facility, structured with a longer term and staged drawdowns from the outset, usually works out cheaper and less stressful.

If you are simply short of a deposit rather than dealing with an unmortgageable property, other options such as a joint venture or a second charge on an existing asset may suit better than bridging. Bridging loans exist to solve a speed or condition problem, not a general shortage of capital, and using them for the wrong reason usually costs more than it needs to.

How to get the best outcome

Get the valuer and solicitor briefed before you commit to a purchase, not after. A same-day desktop valuation can often confirm whether a property is lendable at all before you tie yourself into an auction contract or exchange.

Unmortgageable does not mean unfinanceable. Can you get a bridging loan on a property with no kitchen or bathroom?
Yes, this is one of the most common reasons buyers use bridging loans. Lenders assess the property's current condition and its likely value once works are complete, then lend a percentage of whichever figure is relevant to the loan structure agreed.
What loan-to-value can I expect on an unmortgageable property?
Most bridging lenders offer between 60% and 75% of current value for unmortgageable property, occasionally higher against gross development value for experienced developers with a proven track record of completed projects.

This is the most common reason projects run into trouble. Borrowers should build a genuine contingency of 10-15% into their budget from the outset, since underestimating costs can leave a funding gap mid-project that is expensive to fill.

Yes, bridging loans carry higher rates and fees than mainstream mortgages because they are short-term and higher risk. They are priced for speed and flexibility, not long-term ownership, so refinancing onto a standard mortgage once the property qualifies is usually the sensible exit.
Can first-time developers get bridging loans on unmortgageable property?
